narratives.narrative: The sense (101) is an oath of innocence: 'if there is wrong (evel) in my hands' - wrong named only to be disowned. Type (102) is cognition: this is an act of the mind, a searching self-examination, not a felt state or a deed. Source (103) goes unrecorded - the reading does not trace where the wrong would spring from; it is entertained hypothetically, not attributed. Seat (104) resolves to none: the wrong is not lodged in an organ but held against the whole self. Bearer (105) is the psalmist (inferred): the interior that carries the operation is his own, turned on itself. Operation (106) is the core event - the self submits itself to a conditional self-curse: if I have done this wrong, let the enemy overtake me; a rigorous self-audit staked on integrity. Target (107) is self-imprecation (inferred): the operation aims the curse back at the bearer if guilt is found. Manner (108) is none - no mode is marked; the oath stands plainly. Intensity (109), specifier (110), effect (111) and prohibition (113) are all absent: no degree measured, nothing narrowed, no downstream outcome booked, no forbidding issued - the reading reports the daring examination, not its result. Coupling (112) is oath-if-guilty (inferred): the wrong is bound into a conditional, only real if the self is guilty. Discovery (114) locates it in v3-4, the searching 'if I have done this... if I have repaid my friend with evil'. Role (115) is characteristic; locus (116) is internal:ib-state - the whole movement sits inside as a condition of the moral self. The full process: from no named source, the psalmist's mind turns on itself, dares the worst upon itself should wrong be found in its hands, and rests its whole plea on the integrity that self-audit confirms.
narratives.story: The psalmist does something bold: he puts his own conscience on trial. He names a wrong - and then dares it to be true of him. If I have done this, he says, if there is any crookedness in what my hands have done, if I have paid back a friend with evil, then let my enemy hunt me down and trample me. It is not a feeling but a hard act of self-examination, the mind searching itself without flinching. He never claims the wrong came from anywhere or lives in any part of him; he simply holds the whole self up to the light and stakes everything on being clean. He does not say what the outcome will be - he only makes the daring wager, resting his entire appeal on an integrity he has looked at honestly and found intact.
narratives.variation_note: This is one of two readings of 'wrong' (evel). Here at Psa 7:3 the wrong is entertained by the righteous self as a hypothesis it disowns - a cognition, self-directed, an oath staked on innocence. At Psa 58:2 (H5766:wrong#2) the same word names the actual product of the wicked rulers' hearts. The difference is decisive: the bearer shifts from the upright self examining itself to the corrupt powerful manufacturing injustice, and the movement flips from ascent (integrity confirmed) to descent (injustice devised). The same word marks both the thing the righteous refuses and the thing the wicked produces.

narratives.narrative: The sense (101) is an appeal to be judged on integrity: 'judge me... according to the integrity (tom) that is in me'. Type (102) is volition: an act of the will, integrity offered up to the divine court. Source (103) is unrecorded - the reading does not say whence the integrity comes; it is simply claimed as present. Seat (104) resolves to none: not organ-located but held by the whole person ('that is in me'). Bearer (105) is the psalmist (inferred). Operation (106) is the core event: the self asks God to judge it by its own righteousness and integrity - a confidence so settled it invites, rather than dreads, the verdict. Target (107) is the appeal-to-be-judged (inferred). Manner (108) is none. Intensity (109), specifier (110), effect (111) and prohibition (113) are all absent - no degree, no narrowing, no outcome booked, no forbidding. Coupling (112) is judge-my-integrity (inferred): the integrity is welded to the plea for judgment. Discovery (114) sets it at v8. Role (115) is characteristic; locus (116) is internal:ib-state. The full process: from no named source, the will lifts the integrity it holds within and stakes it before God's tribunal, so sure of its innocence that judgment is sought as vindication.
narratives.story: Most people fear being judged. This man asks for it. Judge me, he says to God - weigh me by my own uprightness, by the wholeness of purpose you will find inside me. He does not explain where that integrity came from or point to any single part of himself; it is simply there, in him, and he is willing to have the whole of it examined. What would terrify a guilty person he welcomes, because he expects the verdict to clear him. His integrity is not something he hides but something he offers up, confident that the closest possible inspection will only prove him right.
narratives.variation_note: First of four readings of 'integrity' (tom). Here at Psa 7:8 integrity is offered to God's court as grounds for a favourable verdict - a volition of confident self-exposure. It differs from Psa 25:21 (integrity pleaded as a preserver in dependence), from Psa 41:12 (integrity gratefully seen to have been honoured by God), and from Psa 101:2 (integrity resolved on as a way of life). Here the accent is on inviting judgment; the same character stands under four different pressures.

narratives.narrative: The sense (101) is 'the upright (yashar) shall behold his face'. Type (102) is affect: the reading reads uprightness by its emotional-relational reward, a longing fulfilled in sight of God. Source (103) is unrecorded. Seat (104) resolves to none - not organ-located; uprightness belongs to the whole person. Bearer (105) is the upright (inferred). Operation (106) is the core event: the LORD is righteous and loves righteous deeds, and the upright shall behold his face - the reward of an upright interior is to see God. Target (107) is the hope-of-seeing-God (inferred). Manner (108) is none. Intensity (109), specifier (110), effect (111) and prohibition (113) are all absent - the reading books no degree, no narrowing, no further outcome, no prohibition. Coupling (112) is behold-his-face (inferred): uprightness is bound to the final vision. Discovery (114) sets it at v7. Role (115) is characteristic; locus (116) is internal:ib-state. The full process: from no named source, the upright interior is oriented not to reward-things but to a final seeing of God; its whole trajectory ends in his face.
narratives.story: The psalm ends not with a prize but with a promise: the upright will see God's face. Everything the wicked aim at the honest heart - their arrows shot in the dark - comes to nothing, because God himself is righteous and loves what is right. And the reward he holds out to the straight-hearted is not treasure or safety but himself: they shall behold his face. The passage does not measure this hope or spell out what follows from it. It simply sets the whole direction of an upright life toward one thing - the sight of God at the end.
narratives.variation_note: First of ten readings of 'upright' (yashar). Here at Psa 11:7 the operation is the final vision of God - uprightness rewarded by seeing his face, read as affect. Across the ten the yashar-heart does many different things: rules over the doomed rich (49:14), exults in heart (64:10), pursues returning justice (94:15), has joy stored for it (97:11), rejoices at God's reversals (107:42), gathers to praise (111:1), sees its line blessed (112:2), receives light in darkness (112:4), and is the object of God's good (125:4). This first reading is distinctive for making the reward a face-to-face seeing rather than a benefit received.

narratives.narrative: The sense (101) is 'shall never be moved' (mot). Type (102) is state: not an act or a feeling but a settled condition. Source (103) is unrecorded - the reading does not trace what supplies the stability, only that it follows the whole preceding conduct. Seat (104) resolves to none: unshakeableness is not organ-located but a property of the person. Bearer (105) is the righteous (inferred) - the one who does all the things the psalm has listed. Operation (106) is the core event: the one who does these things shall never be moved - the settled, unshakeable stability that integrity produces. Target (107) is unshakeableness (inferred). Manner (108) is none. Intensity (109), specifier (110), effect (111) and prohibition (113) are all absent - no degree, no narrowing, no further outcome, no forbidding; the reading names the standing itself. Coupling (112) is never-moved (inferred). Discovery (114) sets it at v5 as the psalm's closing verdict. Role (115) is characteristic; locus (116) is internal:ib-state. The full process: from no named source, the accumulated integrity of the blameless life yields a stability nothing can topple - character become bedrock.
narratives.story: The psalm has just drawn a whole portrait of an honest person - one who speaks truth, does no harm to a neighbour, keeps his word even when it costs him, refuses dirty money. Then it ends with a single verdict: a person like this will never be shaken. It does not explain where the steadiness comes from or what happens next. It simply says that a life built this way becomes unmovable, like bedrock. The integrity is the foundation, and the reward is a stability that nothing can knock down.

narratives.narrative: The sense (101) is 'no usury, no bribe' - integrity read through what it refuses. Type (102) is volition: an act of the will, a deliberate abstention. Source (103) is unrecorded. Seat (104) resolves to none - not organ-located; the refusal belongs to the whole moral person. Bearer (105) is the righteous (inferred). Operation (106) is the core event: he does not lend money at interest or take a bribe against the innocent - integrity worked out in money and in justice. Target (107) is financial-integrity (inferred). Manner (108) is none. Intensity (109), specifier (110), effect (111) and prohibition (113) are all absent: though the content is a refusal, no formal prohibition is booked - the row reads it as the person's own conduct, not a law laid on him; no degree or outcome is scored. Coupling (112) is no-usury-no-bribe (inferred): the two refusals are welded together as one integrity. Discovery (114) sets it at v5. Role (115) is characteristic; locus (116) is internal:ib-state. The full process: from no named source, the will refuses to profit from the vulnerable or to sell a just verdict - integrity shown not in grand deeds but in what it will not do with money and power.
narratives.story: Integrity here shows itself in two refusals. The person who may live in God's presence is one who will not lend money at interest to squeeze the poor, and will not take a bribe to twist a verdict against an innocent person. It is character measured by what it will not do - not by any dramatic act, but by the quiet decision to keep clean hands where money and power meet. He is not obeying a rule imposed from outside; this is simply who he is. The passage does not weigh how hard it is or what he gains by it; it just names the two things a person of integrity refuses to touch.

narratives.narrative: The sense (101) is 'behold your face, satisfied with your likeness'. Type (102) is affect: the reading is carried by longing and its satisfaction. Source (103) is unrecorded. Seat (104) resolves to none - not organ-located; the beholding belongs to the whole self. Bearer (105) is the psalmist (inferred). Operation (106) is the core event: as for the self, it will behold God's face in righteousness and, on waking, be satisfied with his likeness - the true satisfaction, deliberately set against the worldly's fill of treasure and children. Target (107) is God-face-satisfaction (inferred). Manner (108) is none. Intensity (109), specifier (110), effect (111) and prohibition (113) are all absent. Coupling (112) is behold-and-be-satisfied (inferred): the seeing is welded to the satisfying. Discovery (114) sets it at v15 as the counter to v14's men whose portion is in this life. Role (115) is characteristic; locus (116) is internal:ib-state. The full process: from no named source, the righteous self turns from the worldly's plenty and locates its whole satisfaction in the vision of God - beholding his face and being filled by his likeness.
narratives.story: Around the psalmist are people whose whole reward is in this life - full bellies, treasure, children to inherit their wealth. He looks at all of it and turns away. As for me, he says, my satisfaction is somewhere else entirely: I shall see your face, and when I wake I will be filled just by your likeness. His deepest longing is not for things but for the sight of God himself. The passage draws the contrast sharply - their fill of possessions against his fill of God - and leaves it there: the honest heart finds its true contentment in seeing God, not in anything the world can hand it.

narratives.narrative: The sense (101) is 'clean hands, righteousness (tsedeq)'. Type (102) is cognition: the self reckons, reasons about its own record. Source (103) is unrecorded. Seat (104) resolves to none - not organ-located; righteousness and clean hands are held by the whole person. Bearer (105) is the psalmist (inferred). Operation (106) is the core event: the self reckons that God dealt with it according to its righteousness and the cleanness of its hands - a confidence that integrity has been rewarded, the deliverance read as a just response and not arbitrary. Target (107) is integrity-confidence (inferred). Manner (108) is none. Intensity (109), specifier (110), effect (111) and prohibition (113) are all absent. Coupling (112) is clean-hands (inferred): righteousness is welded to the cleanness of the hands, inner rectitude matched by outward act. Discovery (114) sets it at v20. Role (115) is characteristic; locus (116) is internal:ib-state. The full process: from no named source, the mind interprets its rescue as earned by a righteousness it can point to - clean hands and an upright record - reading God's dealing as a measured answer to its own integrity.
narratives.story: Rescued from enemies too strong for him, the psalmist does not treat his deliverance as luck. He reasons it out: God dealt with me like this because of my righteousness, because my hands were clean. He can point to a record - ways kept, God not abandoned - and he reads his rescue as a fair response to it, not an accident. Inner rightness and clean conduct go together in his mind, and he is confident that God noticed and answered them. The passage does not say where that righteousness came from; it simply shows a man reading his own rescue as the just reward of an integrity he knows he kept.
narratives.variation_note: First of four readings of 'righteousness' (H6664, tsedeq). Here at Psa 18:20 righteousness is the self's own confident reckoning that its integrity was rewarded - a cognition. It differs sharply from Psa 45:4 and 45:7, where the same word names the royal-political programme the king advances and loves (a status, with no interior operation), and from Psa 132:9, where righteousness is an investiture put on the priests. Here alone the righteousness is claimed by the self and read back off its own deliverance.

narratives.narrative: The sense (101) is 'blameless (tamim), kept from guilt'. Type (102) is volition: an act of the will, self kept clear of sin. Source (103) is unrecorded. Seat (104) resolves to none - the blamelessness is held by the whole self, not an organ. Bearer (105) is the psalmist (inferred). Operation (106) is the core event: the self was blameless before God and kept itself from its own guilt - a vigilant self-guarding, not merely keeping God's ways outwardly but policing the self away from its own iniquity. Target (107) is self-guarding (inferred). Manner (108) is none. Intensity (109), specifier (110), effect (111) and prohibition (113) are all absent. Coupling (112) is keep-from-guilt (inferred): blamelessness is welded to the active keeping-away from guilt. Discovery (114) sets it at v23, where the operation turns inward. Role (115) is characteristic; locus (116) is internal:ib-state. The full process: from no named source, the will stands blameless before God by guarding the self against its own guilt - integrity maintained as an inward vigilance.
narratives.story: Being blameless, here, is not a happy accident - it is work the psalmist does on himself. I was blameless before God, he says, and I kept myself from my own guilt. The key word is 'kept': he is standing guard over himself, watching that he does not drift into wrongdoing. It is not just about obeying God's rules on the outside; it is an inward policing, a refusal to let guilt get a foothold. The passage does not say where he found the strength for it or what came of it. It simply shows a man holding himself clear of sin by keeping constant watch over his own heart.
narratives.variation_note: First of five readings of 'blameless' (tamim). Here at Psa 18:23 blamelessness is an active inward self-guarding - the will keeping the self from its own guilt (a volition). It differs from Psa 101:2 (blamelessness pondered and resolved on as a way of life), Psa 101:6 (blamelessness as the criterion that qualifies others for the king's household), Psa 119:1 (blamelessness pronounced blessed in a beatitude), and Psa 119:80 (blamelessness of heart pleaded for). Here alone it is read as vigilant self-policing against guilt.

narratives.narrative: The sense (101) is 'we rise and stand upright' (qum). Type (102) is state: a settled standing, not an act or a feeling. Source (103) is unrecorded - the reading does not name what holds them up, though the psalm has just contrasted trust in chariots with trust in the LORD's name. Seat (104) resolves to none: the standing belongs to the whole company, not an organ. Bearer (105) is the people (inferred) - the God-trusting community. Operation (106) is the core event: they collapse and fall, but we rise and stand upright - the steadfast standing of those who trust God, set against the chariot-trusters who fall. Target (107) is steadfastness (inferred). Manner (108) is none. Intensity (109), specifier (110), effect (111) and prohibition (113) are all absent. Coupling (112) is rise-and-stand (inferred): the rising is welded to the standing. Discovery (114) sets it at v8 as the contrast between the fallen and the standing. Role (115) is characteristic; locus (116) is internal:ib-state. The full process: from no named source, the trusting community, where others topple, rises and holds its feet - integrity of trust shown as an enduring, upright standing.
narratives.story: Two kinds of people are set side by side. Some put their confidence in chariots and horses - in raw military strength - and when the test comes, they buckle and fall. The others trust in the name of their God, and where the first collapse, these rise and stand on their feet. The passage does not spell out what keeps them standing, though the whole song has just said it is the Lord and not the war-machine. It simply draws the picture: the ones who lean on God are the ones left upright when everything around them goes down. Their steadiness is the visible proof of where their trust was placed.

narratives.narrative: The sense (101) is 'clean hands and a pure (bar) heart'. Type (102) is state: a settled condition of purity, not an act. Source (103) is unrecorded. Seat (104) resolves to none for the term itself, though the verse pairs the pure heart with clean hands - the reading treats purity as a state of the whole person rather than an isolated organ. Bearer (105) is the worshipper (inferred) - the one who would ascend God's hill. Operation (106) is the core event: the one who may ascend has clean hands and a pure heart - integrity of deed matched by integrity of the inner self, a doubled purity. Target (107) is purity (inferred). Manner (108) is none. Intensity (109), specifier (110), effect (111) and prohibition (113) are all absent. Coupling (112) is clean-hands-pure-heart (inferred): the outward act and the inward heart are welded as one qualification. Discovery (114) sets it at v4, naming the qualification for God's presence. Role (115) is characteristic; locus (116) is internal:ib-state. The full process: from no named source, purity is the condition that opens the way up to God - hands undefiled in deed and heart undefiled within, the two held together as the single requirement.
narratives.story: Who is allowed to climb God's holy hill and stand in his presence? The psalm answers with two things held together: clean hands and a pure heart. It is not enough to act rightly on the outside if the inside is corrupt, and it is not enough to feel pure within if the hands are dirty. Both must be clean - the deed and the heart, matching each other. The passage does not say how a person gets this purity or what follows from it; it simply names it as the single condition for coming near to God. Purity, inside and out, is the door.
narratives.variation_note: First of two readings of 'pure' (bar). Here at Psa 24:4 purity is the entrance-qualification for God's presence - a state, deed and heart together, read as the door to the holy hill. At Psa 73:1 (H1249:pure#2) the same word names the creed the doubting psalmist clings to - that God is good to the pure in heart - a truth defended against the scandal of the wicked's prosperity. Here purity opens the way up; there it is the belief that nearly broke under experience.

narratives.narrative: The sense (101) is 'integrity and uprightness preserve me' (tom). Type (102) is volition: an act of the will, integrity summoned as a guard. Source (103) is unrecorded. Seat (104) resolves to none - held by the whole self. Bearer (105) is the psalmist (inferred). Operation (106) is the core event: the self asks that integrity and uprightness preserve it, for it waits on God - character offered as its own protection, yet held in dependence. Target (107) is integrity (inferred). Manner (108) is none. Intensity (109), specifier (110), effect (111) and prohibition (113) are all absent. Coupling (112) is integrity-preserve (inferred): integrity is welded to the act of preserving, the guard the self leans on. Discovery (114) sets it at v21. Role (115) is characteristic; locus (116) is internal:ib-state. The full process: from no named source, the will offers up its own integrity - not as self-sufficiency but bound to waiting on God - and asks that this character stand guard over it in its distress.
narratives.story: Surrounded by enemies and pleading to be delivered, the psalmist reaches for one thing to shield him: his own integrity. May integrity and uprightness keep me safe, he prays - and in the same breath adds, for I wait for you. So it is not a boast of self-sufficiency. He is offering the wholeness of his own character as a kind of guard, but he holds it out to God, leaning on him at the same time. The passage does not explain where the integrity comes from; it simply shows a man in trouble asking that the honesty of his own life stand between him and harm, while he waits on God to act.
narratives.variation_note: Second of four readings of 'integrity' (tom). Here at Psa 25:21 integrity is pleaded as a preserver - a guard the self leans on while waiting on God. It differs from Psa 7:8 (integrity offered to God's court, inviting judgment), Psa 41:12 (integrity gratefully seen already honoured by God), and Psa 101:2 (integrity resolved on as a way of life). Here alone integrity is asked to do the protecting.

narratives.narrative: The sense (101) is 'the righteous (tsaddiq) utters wisdom'. Type (102) is cognition: uniquely among the tsaddiq readings, this one is read through the interior's thought welling into speech. Source (103) is unrecorded. Seat (104) resolves to none for the term, though the verse names heart and mouth - the reading treats the wise speech as flowing from the whole shaped interior, not one organ. Bearer (105) is the righteous (inferred). Operation (106) is the core event: the mouth of the righteous utters wisdom and his tongue speaks justice - an interior so shaped that wise, just speech pours out of it. Target (107) is wise-speech (inferred). Manner (108) is none. Intensity (109), specifier (110), effect (111) and prohibition (113) are all absent. Coupling (112) is utter-wisdom (inferred): righteousness is welded to the wisdom the mouth pours out. Discovery (114) sets it at v30, with v31 grounding it - the law of God is in his heart. Role (115) is characteristic; locus (116) is internal:ib-state. The full process: from no named source, the righteous interior, carrying God's law in the heart, overflows into wise and just speech - what the heart holds, the mouth speaks.
narratives.story: The righteous person is known here by what comes out of his mouth. Because God's law lives in his heart, his speech carries wisdom and his words deal out justice. It is not a trick of eloquence but an overflow: a heart shaped by what is right cannot help but speak what is right. The passage traces the flow from inside to outside - the law stored in the heart, then wisdom and justice on the tongue. It does not measure how much or say what results; it simply shows that a rightly-formed inner life pours itself out in good and true words.
narratives.variation_note: One of seventeen readings of 'righteous' (tsaddiq), and distinctive: nearly all the others read the tsaddiq as a status or community that receives something (joy, light, vindication, stability). Here at Psa 37:30 alone the righteous is read as cognition - an active interior whose stored law overflows into wise, just speech. It is the tsaddiq as producer of good words, not recipient of reward.

narratives.narrative: The sense (101) is 'you uphold me because of my integrity' (tom). Type (102) is affect: read through the confident feeling of being honoured. Source (103) is unrecorded. Seat (104) resolves to none - held by the whole self. Bearer (105) is the psalmist (inferred). Operation (106) is the core event: God has upheld the self because of its integrity and set it in his presence forever - integrity that God himself sustains and stations before his face. Target (107) is upheld-integrity (inferred). Manner (108) is none. Intensity (109), specifier (110), effect (111) and prohibition (113) are all absent. Coupling (112) is upheld-for-integrity (inferred): the integrity is welded to God's upholding, cause and effect bound together. Discovery (114) sets it at v12. Role (115) is characteristic; locus (116) is internal:ib-state. The full process: from no named source, the self's integrity becomes the reason God holds it up - betrayed by a friend and surrounded by malice, it reads God's sustaining and its permanent place before his face as the honouring of its own uprightness.
narratives.story: Betrayed by a close friend and whispered about by enemies who want him dead, the psalmist finds one solid thing to stand on: God has held me up because of my integrity. He does not claim to have engineered his own rescue. He sees his uprightness as the reason God sustained him and gave him a permanent place in his presence. The feeling is confidence - not that he is flawless, but that his honesty was seen and honoured. The passage does not explain where the integrity came from; it simply shows a man reading God's steady support, and his lasting place before God's face, as the reward of a life kept whole.
narratives.variation_note: Third of four readings of 'integrity' (tom). Here at Psa 41:12 integrity is gratefully recognized as the reason God has already upheld the self - an affect of honoured confidence, looking back. It differs from Psa 7:8 (integrity offered forward to God's judgment), Psa 25:21 (integrity pleaded as a preserver mid-crisis), and Psa 101:2 (integrity resolved on as future conduct). Here alone the integrity is seen as already vindicated by God's sustaining hand.

narratives.narrative: The sense (101) is 'righteousness (tsedeq)' - the third virtue of the king's victorious ride, alongside truth and meekness. Type (102) is status: righteousness as a standing quality of the reign, not an interior act. Source (103) is unrecorded. Seat (104) resolves to none. Bearer (105) is the king, or rather his cause (inferred). Operation (106) is none: the reading explicitly finds no operation - righteousness here is not something the interior does but a banner the king advances; the silence marks it as a programmatic quality rather than a movement of the heart. Target (107) is likewise none. Manner (108) is none. Intensity (109), specifier (110), effect (111) and prohibition (113) are all absent. Coupling (112) is a span-pairing: righteousness set with truth and meekness (v4) as the moral cause the king rides out for. Discovery (114) names it the moral programme of his reign, echoed in v7's love of righteousness. Role (115) is characteristic; locus (116) is internal:ib-state. The full process: with no interior operation or target recorded, righteousness stands as one of three causes the king embodies and advances - a public, political rectitude paired with truth and meekness, the moral programme his rule exists to establish.
narratives.story: As the king rides out in his splendour, the psalm names what he is fighting for: truth, meekness, and righteousness. This righteousness is not described as a feeling or an inner struggle - it is a cause, a banner, the moral order his whole reign is meant to establish. It stands beside truth and gentleness as the three things his victory serves. The passage does not show it happening inside him so much as flying above him as his purpose. It is the rightness a good king exists to bring about in his kingdom - the programme of his rule, echoed later when the song says he loves righteousness and hates wickedness.
narratives.variation_note: Second of four readings of 'righteousness' (H6664, tsedeq), and one of two in Psalm 45. Here at v4 righteousness is a cause the king rides out to advance - paired with truth and meekness, read as status with no interior operation. At v7 (H6664:righteousnes#3) the same word becomes the object of the king's love ('you have loved righteousness'). The difference: here righteousness is the programme advanced; there it is the thing the royal heart is set on. Both differ from Psa 18:20 (righteousness as the self's own vindication) and Psa 132:9 (righteousness as priestly investiture).

narratives.narrative: The sense (101) is 'righteousness (tsedeq) - loved' - 'you have loved righteousness and hated wickedness'. Type (102) is status: righteousness as the moral order the king's heart is set on. Source (103) is unrecorded. Seat (104) resolves to none. Bearer (105) is righteousness itself, as the object of the king's love (inferred). Operation (106) is none - as in v4, the reading finds no interior operation; but here the silence is telling, for the loving is the king's act and righteousness is what that love reaches for. Target (107) is none. Manner (108) is none. Intensity (109), specifier (110), effect (111) and prohibition (113) are all absent. Coupling (112) is a span-pairing: righteousness as the object of the king's love (v7), set against the wickedness he hates. Discovery (114) names it the right the king cherishes, the moral order his heart is set on, recurring from v4. Role (115) is characteristic; locus (116) is internal:ib-state. The full process: with no interior operation recorded of righteousness itself, it stands as the thing the king loves - his affection fixed on the right and turned away from the wicked; righteousness as the settled orientation of a royal heart.
narratives.story: The psalm says something simple and weighty about the king's heart: he loves righteousness and hates wickedness. Righteousness here is not something he does so much as something he is drawn to - the moral order his affections are fixed on. Set against the evil he turns away from, it marks the whole bent of his inner life: what he cherishes, what he wants the world to be. The passage does not describe the feeling working itself out; it simply names righteousness as the object of a king's love, and in doing so tells you what kind of ruler he is - one whose heart is set on what is right.
narratives.variation_note: Third of four readings of 'righteousness' (H6664, tsedeq), the second in Psalm 45. Here at v7 righteousness is the object of the king's love - what his heart is set on. It differs from v4 (H6664:righteousnes#2), where the same word is a cause he advances in battle. The finding: at v4 righteousness is the programme ridden out for; at v7 it is the affection behind the programme. Together they show the king loving what he then fights to establish.

narratives.narrative: The sense (101) is 'upright (yashar)'. Type (102) is status: the upright as a standing class, set over against the doomed rich. Source (103) is unrecorded. Seat (104) resolves to none. Bearer (105) is the upright (inferred). Operation (106) is the core event: they rule over them in the morning - the upright's dawn-triumph over the wealthy consigned to Sheol. Target (107) is the doomed rich (inferred) - those whose shepherd is death. Manner (108) is none. Intensity (109), specifier (110), effect (111) and prohibition (113) are all absent. Coupling (112) is none - no further weld is recorded; the reversal stands alone. Discovery (114) sets it at v14 as the final reversal: the just prevailing over the rich whom death shepherds. Role (115) is characteristic; locus (116) is internal:ib-state. The full process: from no named source, the upright - who owned little and trusted God rather than wealth - come to rule at daybreak over the rich who trusted their riches and are led like sheep to the grave; integrity outlasts wealth and inherits the morning.
narratives.story: The psalm has been watching the rich - people who trust their money and boast of it, sure they will live forever. But death is their shepherd; like sheep they are herded down to the grave, and all their wealth stays behind. Then comes the turn: in the morning, the upright will rule over them. The honest, who owned little and leaned on God instead of their bank accounts, outlast the wealthy and come out on top when the new day breaks. The passage does not dwell on how; it simply sets the picture - riches herded into the dark, integrity rising to rule at dawn.
narratives.variation_note: Second of ten readings of 'upright' (yashar), and distinctive for its operation: here at Psa 49:14 the upright actively rule over others - the doomed rich - in a dawn reversal. Most yashar readings show the upright receiving something (light, joy, blessing) or rejoicing; this one alone gives them dominion over the wicked. The variation carries the psalm's whole argument: wealth ends in the grave, but integrity ends in rule.

narratives.narrative: The sense (101) is 'clean / pure (tahor) - create in me a clean heart'. Type (102) is status: a state of purity, here sought at its very source. Source (103) is unrecorded. Seat (104) is the heart - uniquely for this family, the purity is organ-located, lodged in the heart (v10). Bearer (105) is the penitent (inferred). Operation (106) is the core event: the clean heart is created (bara) anew in him - not repaired but made fresh. Target (107) is none recorded - the operation is the making itself. Manner (108) is by divine creation (bara): the same verb that made the world, marking that native iniquity cannot be merely washed but must be re-created. Intensity (109), specifier (110), effect (111) and prohibition (113) are all absent. Coupling (112) is a span-pairing: the clean heart paired with the renewed right spirit (v10). Discovery (114) names it the psalm's turning-point: not repair but new creation, because the iniquity of v5 goes to the source. Role (115) is characteristic; locus (116) is internal:heart. The full process: from no named source in the self, the penitent asks God to create a clean heart at the very root - purity that must be made, not mended, and paired with a renewed steadfast spirit within.
narratives.story: Deep in his confession, the psalmist reaches the bottom of the problem. It is not enough to be washed on the surface; the trouble is in the heart itself, and it goes all the way back to his beginning. So he asks for something drastic: create in me a clean heart. Not clean me up, not patch me - create, the same word used for making the world out of nothing. He is asking God to make a new heart where the old one is corrupt, and to put a steady, willing spirit inside him along with it. The purity he wants is not a repair job but a fresh act of creation, right at the root of who he is.

narratives.narrative: The sense (101) is 'cleanse / purify (taher) - cleanse me from sin'. Type (102) is status: a state of cleanness longed for. Source (103) is unrecorded. Seat (104) resolves to none - the cleansing is asked for the whole self, not an organ. Bearer (105) is the penitent, longing to be clean (inferred). Operation (106) is the core event: the penitent longs for and pleads to be cleansed. Target (107) is 'from sin' (inferred) - the defilement to be removed. Manner (108) is none. Intensity (109), specifier (110), effect (111) and prohibition (113) are all absent. Coupling (112) is a span-pairing: this purity-longing renewed at v7 ('I shall be clean'). Discovery (114) names it the Miserere's driving hunger - not merely to be pardoned but to be made pure, the deep desire that runs through the whole psalm. Role (115) is characteristic; locus (116) is internal:ib-state. The full process: from no named source, the penitent's whole inner longing reaches past forgiveness toward cleanness - a hunger to be purified of sin itself, the desire that drives the psalm.
narratives.story: The psalmist wants more than to be let off. Cleanse me from my sin, he prays - not just forgive the debt but wash out the stain. Running underneath the whole prayer is a deep hunger not simply to be pardoned but to be made genuinely pure. He longs for it the way a person longs for water. The passage does not measure the longing or say how it is answered here; it simply lays bare the craving at the heart of the confession - to be cleansed, made new, purged of the sin itself. It is the desire that drives everything else he asks for.

narratives.narrative: The sense (101) is 'be clean / pure (taher) - I shall be clean'. Type (102) is status: the cleansed state itself. Source (103) is unrecorded. Seat (104) resolves to none - the cleanness belongs to the whole self. Bearer (105) is the penitent (inferred). Operation (106) is the core event: the penitent is made clean. Target (107) is none - the operation is the becoming-clean itself. Manner (108) is 'whiter than snow': the cleanness is intensified past the whiteness of snow, purity beyond the ordinary. Intensity (109), specifier (110), effect (111) and prohibition (113) are all absent as separate rows - though 'whiter than snow' carries the force, it is booked under manner, not degree. Coupling (112) is a span-pairing: the cleansing longed for back in v2. Discovery (114) names it the purity that answers the plea - the state the created clean heart of v10 reaches toward. Role (115) is characteristic; locus (116) is internal:ib-state. The full process: from no named source, the penitent's longing to be cleansed is answered in a state whiter than snow - purity received, the goal toward which the whole confession strains.
narratives.story: Here the longing turns into a picture of the result. Wash me, the psalmist says, and I shall be clean - whiter than snow. This is the purity he has been aching for: not a grey, half-cleaned conscience but something dazzlingly white, cleaner than fresh snowfall. It answers the plea he made earlier to be washed from his sin, and it is the very thing his prayer for a new heart is straining toward. The passage does not analyse it; it simply holds up the image - a soul made clean past the whiteness of snow - as the goal the whole confession is reaching for.

narratives.narrative: The sense (101) is 'righteous ones (tsaddiq) - the righteous shall see'. Type (102) is status: the righteous as the God-fearing community. Source (103) is unrecorded. Seat (104) resolves to none. Bearer (105) is the righteous (inferred). Operation (106) is the core event: they see the tyrant's fall. Target (107) is none recorded - the seeing is the movement. Manner (108) is none. Intensity (109), specifier (110), effect (111) and prohibition (113) are all absent. Coupling (112) is a span-pairing: their seeing issues in fear and derisive laughter (v6-7). Discovery (114) names them the God-fearing who witness the boaster's overthrow, the counter-company to the man who trusted his riches. Role (115) is characteristic; locus (116) is external:person - notably, the reading places the righteous outward, as a visible community rather than an inner state. The full process: from no named source, the righteous community watches the tyrant broken by God, and their seeing turns to awe and then to laughter at the man who made wealth, not God, his refuge - integrity vindicated as spectator to the fall of arrogance.
narratives.story: A boastful, powerful man has built his life on his money and his cutting tongue, mocking God. Then God breaks him - uproots him for good. And the righteous are there to see it. They watch the great man fall, and their watching turns first to a holy fear and then to laughter: look at the man who would not make God his refuge but trusted his pile of riches. The passage shows the honest community as witnesses to arrogance collapsing. They are not the ones who bring him down; they simply see it happen, and in their seeing the whole point of the story lands - trust your wealth against God, and this is how it ends.
narratives.variation_note: One of seventeen readings of 'righteous' (tsaddiq). Here at Psa 52:6 the righteous are witnesses to the wicked's fall, their seeing issuing in fear and laughter - and notably placed as external:person, an outward community rather than an inner state. It shares the 'see the judgment' motif with Psa 58:10 and 64:10, but here the response is uniquely doubled into awe and derision.

narratives.narrative: The sense (101) is 'righteous (tsaddiq) - never permit the righteous to be moved'. Type (102) is status. Source (103) is unrecorded. Seat (104) resolves to none. Bearer (105) is the righteous (inferred). Operation (106) is the core event: the righteous is kept from being moved - held unshaken by God. Target (107) is none recorded. Manner (108) is 'never to be shaken' - the stability is absolute. Intensity (109), specifier (110), effect (111) and prohibition (113) are all absent. Coupling (112) is a span-pairing: the righteous here is the one who casts his burden on the LORD (v22). Discovery (114) names it the settled security of the God-truster - the promised stability that answers the psalm's terror of betrayal, the opposite of the treacherous who will not live out half their days. Role (115) is characteristic; locus (116) is internal:ib-state. The full process: from no named source in the self, the righteous - having cast his burden on God - is held unmovable; integrity's reward is a God-given steadiness set against the collapse promised to the men of blood and treachery.
narratives.story: The psalm is full of dread - a trusted friend has turned traitor, his smooth words hiding drawn swords. Into that fear comes a promise: cast your burden on the Lord, and he will never let the righteous be shaken. The honest person who hands his weight over to God is held steady, unmovable, no matter what the betrayers do. And the contrast is stark - the treacherous will not live out half their days, but the one who trusts God stays standing. The passage does not explain the mechanics; it simply promises that integrity, leaning its whole load on God, is kept from ever being toppled.
narratives.variation_note: One of seventeen readings of 'righteous' (tsaddiq). Here at Psa 55:22 the righteous is kept unshaken by God - a stability welded to the act of casting one's burden on the LORD. It shares the 'never moved' promise with Psa 112:6, but here it is set directly against betrayal and the short life of the treacherous, making the steadiness an answer to terror rather than a general blessing.

narratives.narrative: The sense (101) is 'wrongs / injustice (evel) - you devise wrongs'. Type (102) is status: injustice as the settled product of corrupt hearts. Source (103) is unrecorded as a separate row, though the verse locates the devising 'in your hearts'. Seat (104) resolves to none for the term itself. Bearer (105) is the unjust rulers (inferred) - the 'gods' who should judge uprightly. Operation (106) is the core event: the wrongs are devised - manufactured in the heart. Target (107) is none recorded. Manner (108) is none. Intensity (109), specifier (110), effect (111) and prohibition (113) are all absent. Coupling (112) is a span-pairing: the devised wrongs paired with the violence the hands deal out (v2). Discovery (114) names it the injustice that is the rulers' true product - the very opposite of the righteousness they were charged to decree (v1). Role (115) is characteristic; locus (116) is internal:ib-state - the wrong is generated within, in the heart, before the hands deal it out. The full process: from corrupt interiors, the rulers who should decree what is right instead devise injustice in their hearts and mete out violence with their hands - integrity's exact inversion, wrong produced where righteousness was owed.
narratives.story: These are rulers whose job was to judge fairly - and they do the opposite. The psalm exposes what is really going on inside them: in your hearts you devise wrongs. The injustice is not an accident or a slip; it is manufactured, planned in the heart before it ever reaches the hands, which then deal out violence across the land. They were meant to decree what is right, and instead they invent what is crooked. The passage shows integrity turned exactly inside out - the same inner workshop that should produce justice churning out injustice instead. The wrong starts within and flows outward into the world as violence.
narratives.variation_note: Second of two readings of 'wrong' (evel). Here at Psa 58:2 the wrong is the actual product of the corrupt rulers' hearts - a status, devised within and dealt out as violence. It inverts Psa 7:3 (H5766:wrong#1), where the same word is a hypothesis the righteous self disowns under oath. The bearer shifts from the upright self examining itself to the wicked powerful manufacturing injustice; the movement flips from ascent (integrity confirmed) to descent (injustice produced). The one word marks both what the righteous refuses and what the wicked make.

narratives.narrative: The sense (101) is 'righteous (tsaddiq) - the righteous will rejoice'. Type (102) is status. Source (103) is unrecorded. Seat (104) resolves to none. Bearer (105) is the righteous (inferred). Operation (106) is the core event: they see God's vengeance. Target (107) is none recorded. Manner (108) is none. Intensity (109), specifier (110), effect (111) and prohibition (113) are all absent. Coupling (112) is a span-pairing: the seeing issues in rejoicing at the vengeance (v10). Discovery (114) names them the upright vindicated at last, their faith confirmed when justice falls on the wicked - the counterpart to the corrupt rulers of the psalm's opening. Role (115) is characteristic; locus (116) is external:person - the righteous read outward, as a community seen to rejoice. The full process: from no named source, the righteous witness God's judgment on the wicked and their seeing turns to rejoicing; integrity's vindication is to watch justice finally done, the dark reward of seeing the corrupt overthrown named without flinching.
narratives.story: After a psalm raging against corrupt judges, the ending is blunt: the righteous will rejoice when he sees God take vengeance. The honest person, who has lived under injustice, watches justice finally fall on the wicked - and he is glad. The image is fierce, even uncomfortable; the passage does not soften it. Faith that had been strained by watching the corrupt get away with everything is confirmed the moment they are brought down. There is a reward for living right after all, and a God who really does judge the earth. The righteous rejoices not in cruelty for its own sake but in seeing the moral order restored at last.
narratives.variation_note: One of seventeen readings of 'righteous' (tsaddiq). Here at Psa 58:10 the righteous rejoice at seeing God's vengeance on the wicked - placed as external:person and read at full, uncomfortable weight (the vindicated upright glad at the fall of the corrupt). It shares the 'see the judgment and rejoice' motif with Psa 52:6 and 64:10, but here the vindication is the fiercest, answering a psalm consumed with judicial corruption.

narratives.narrative: The sense (101) is 'blameless / complete (tam) - shooting at the blameless'. Type (102) is status: the blameless as an innocent standing, here the target of malice. Source (103) is unrecorded. Seat (104) resolves to none. Bearer (105) is the psalmist, the innocent target (inferred). Operation (106) is the core event: the blameless one is shot at from ambush. Target (107) is none recorded. Manner (108) is 'suddenly, from ambush' - the attack is treacherous, without warning. Intensity (109), specifier (110), effect (111) and prohibition (113) are all absent. Coupling (112) is none - no further weld is recorded; the innocence stands stark against the ambush. Discovery (114) names the point: the innocence of the target is what makes the ambush the more wicked - he is attacked not for any fault but simply as the object of malice, shot at without fear. Role (115) is characteristic; locus (116) is internal:ib-state. The full process: from no named source, the blameless interior is set upon by hidden attackers - integrity here is not rewarded but assaulted, the guiltless made a mark precisely because he is guiltless; the reading reports the innocent suffering without filtering the discomfort.
narratives.story: The victim in this psalm has done nothing wrong - that is exactly the point. He is blameless, and the wicked shoot at him from hiding anyway, aiming their bitter words like arrows, striking suddenly and without a flicker of fear. His innocence does not protect him; if anything it makes the attack uglier, because there is no cause for it at all. He is simply a target for people who love malice. The passage does not pretend integrity always shields a person from harm. Here it shows the opposite - the honest man ambushed precisely because he is honest, hunted by those who plot in the dark against someone who never gave them a reason.

narratives.narrative: The sense (101) is 'upright (yashar) - all the upright in heart'. Type (102) is status. Source (103) is unrecorded. Seat (104) is the heart (span-linked) - here the uprightness is located in the heart, set against the deep-hidden hearts of the plotters (v6). Bearer (105) is the upright (inferred). Operation (106) is the core event: they exult (span-linked to v10). Target (107) is none recorded. Manner (108) is 'in heart' - the exultation rises from the same heart named as the seat. Intensity (109), specifier (110), effect (111) and prohibition (113) are all absent. Coupling (112) is a span-pairing: the upright in heart paired with the righteous rejoicing (v10). Discovery (114) names them the straight-hearted, over against the covert depths of the plotters - openness before God as the opposite of the wicked's hidden schemes, called to exult at his vindication. Role (115) is characteristic; locus (116) is internal:heart. The full process: from no named source, the upright heart - open where the wicked's is hidden - breaks into exultation as God brings the plotters to ruin; integrity read as a transparent heart that rejoices in the light while the schemers are undone by their own tongues.
narratives.story: The wicked in this psalm work in secret - deep, hidden hearts plotting ambushes and asking, 'who will see us?' Then God turns their own tongues against them and brings them down. And the response of the upright is joy that rises straight from the heart: let all the upright in heart exult! The contrast is the whole point - the schemers' hearts are covered and dark; the upright heart is open, straight, with nothing to hide. When God sets things right, that open heart bursts into celebration. The passage shows integrity as a kind of transparency before God, and its natural reaction to seeing justice done is unguarded gladness.
narratives.variation_note: Third of ten readings of 'upright' (yashar). Here at Psa 64:10 the operation is heartfelt exultation, and uniquely the seat is named - the heart - set explicitly against the hidden hearts of the plotters. Where other yashar readings show the upright receiving benefits, this one contrasts an open heart with concealed ones and reads uprightness as transparency before God that overflows in joy at his vindication.

narratives.narrative: The sense (101) is 'righteous (tsaddiq) - let the righteous rejoice'. Type (102) is status. Source (103) is unrecorded. Seat (104) resolves to none. Bearer (105) is the righteous one (inferred). Operation (106) is the core event: rejoice and take refuge (span-linked to v10). Target (107) is none recorded. Manner (108) is none. Intensity (109), specifier (110), effect (111) and prohibition (113) are all absent. Coupling (112) is a span-pairing: the righteous one paired with the upright in heart (v10). Discovery (114) names him the vindicated upright, over against the fallen plotters, called to rejoice and take refuge as the wicked are brought to ruin. Role (115) is characteristic; locus (116) is external:person. The full process: from no named source, the righteous responds to the plotters' downfall with a double movement - rejoicing in the LORD and taking refuge in him; integrity's response to vindication is not only joy but a renewed running to God for shelter.
narratives.story: When the plotters are brought to ruin by their own schemes and all mankind stands in awe of what God has done, the righteous person does two things at once: he rejoices, and he takes refuge. He is glad, of course, to see God set things right - but his gladness is not a victory dance so much as a deeper leaning into God himself. Vindication does not make him self-satisfied; it sends him running back to the shelter of the God who saved him. The passage pairs him with everyone else who is upright in heart, and shows integrity responding to rescue with both celebration and renewed trust.
narratives.variation_note: One of seventeen readings of 'righteous' (tsaddiq), sharing Psa 64:10 with the yashar reading above. Here the righteous both rejoice and take refuge - a doubled response that adds trust to joy, distinguishing it from the 'see and rejoice' readings (52:6, 58:10) where the accent falls on witnessing judgment. Placed as external:person and paired with the upright in heart, it reads vindication as an occasion for renewed sheltering in God.

narratives.narrative: The sense (101) is 'righteous (tsaddiq) - the righteous shall be glad'. Type (102) is status. Source (103) is unrecorded. Seat (104) resolves to none. Bearer (105) is the righteous (inferred). Operation (106) is the core event: be glad and exult (span-linked, v3). Target (107) is 'before God' (inferred) - the joy is directed Godward. Manner (108) is 'jubilant with joy' - the gladness is heaped high. Intensity (109), specifier (110), effect (111) and prohibition (113) are all absent as separate rows, though the fourfold piling of joy-words carries the force. Coupling (112) is a span-pairing: the fourfold joy - glad, exult, jubilant, joy (v3). Discovery (114) names it the fourfold gladness of the upright, over against the melting wicked - the righteous whose response to God's rising is overflowing joy heaped in four verbs. Role (115) is characteristic; locus (116) is external:god - the joy is oriented toward God. The full process: from no named source, as God arises and the wicked melt like wax, the righteous respond with a joy so full it takes four words to hold it - gladness, exultation, jubilation - all poured out before God; integrity's response to God's triumph is uncontainable rejoicing.
narratives.story: God arises, and his enemies scatter like smoke, melting away like wax before fire. In the same moment the righteous do the opposite of melting - they overflow with joy. The psalm can hardly find enough words for it: they are glad, they exult, they are jubilant, they shout for joy, all of it poured out before God. Where the wicked dissolve, the upright blaze up with celebration. The passage does not measure or explain the joy; it simply piles word on word to show how full it is. Integrity's answer to seeing God triumph is not quiet relief but uncontainable, overflowing gladness.
narratives.variation_note: One of seventeen readings of 'righteous' (tsaddiq). Here at Psa 68:3 the accent is the sheer volume of joy - a fourfold heaping of glad/exult/jubilant/joy, oriented Godward (external:god), set against the melting wicked. Where other tsaddiq joy-readings note a single response, this one is distinguished by its overflowing, piled-up quality: integrity's rejoicing at its fullest.

narratives.narrative: The sense (101) is 'justice (mishpat) - give the king your justice'. Type (102) is status: justice as a ruling endowment. Source (103) is unrecorded as a separate row, though the verse names God as giver. Seat (104) resolves to none. Bearer (105) is the king, endowed by God (inferred). Operation (106) is the core event: justice is given by God, to rule with. Target (107) is 'for judging the people' (inferred). Manner (108) is none. Intensity (109), specifier (110), effect (111) and prohibition (113) are all absent. Coupling (112) is a span-pairing: justice to the king paired with righteousness to the royal son (v1). Discovery (114) names it the prayer that the ruler be endowed with God's own justice - divine justice becoming the king's ruling character, the foundation of the ideal reign. Role (115) is characteristic; locus (116) is external:person. The full process: with no interior struggle recorded, justice is prayed down from God into the king to become his ruling character - the just governance he must receive in order to judge the people rightly, especially the poor; integrity here is a governing capacity received, not self-generated.
narratives.story: The psalm opens with a prayer for a king, and the first thing it asks for is not power or wealth but justice: give the king your justice, O God. Real justice, the psalm assumes, is not something a ruler manufactures on his own - it has to be received from God and become the very character he governs by. Paired with it is righteousness for the royal son. Together they are the foundation of a good reign: with God's own justice inside him, the king can judge the people fairly and defend the poor. The passage does not show the king wrestling toward this; it shows it prayed down into him as the gift that makes a true ruler.
narratives.variation_note: First of three readings of 'justice' (mishpat). Here at Psa 72:1 justice is a governing endowment prayed down from God into the king - placed as external:person, paired with righteousness. It differs from Psa 106:3 (justice kept constantly by the blessed) and Psa 112:5 (justice practised in a man's private dealings). Here alone justice is received-to-rule-with rather than a habit of ordinary conduct.

narratives.narrative: The sense (101) is 'righteousness (tsedaqah) - your righteousness to the royal son'. Type (102) is status: righteousness as a royal endowment. Source (103) is unrecorded as a separate row, though God is the giver. Seat (104) resolves to none. Bearer (105) is the royal son, endowed by God (inferred). Operation (106) is the core event: righteousness is given by God. Target (107) is none recorded. Manner (108) is none. Intensity (109), specifier (110), effect (111) and prohibition (113) are all absent. Coupling (112) is a span-pairing: righteousness to the royal son paired with justice to the king (v1). Discovery (114) names it the moral rectitude the king must receive from God - the righteousness that makes him judge the poor justly, God's righteousness given to be the ruler's own, the mark of the true king. Role (115) is characteristic; locus (116) is external:person. The full process: with no interior operation of the son's own recorded, righteousness is prayed down from God to become the royal son's character - the rectitude that, joined to justice, equips him to rule the poor rightly; integrity as a governing endowment received from above.
narratives.story: Alongside the prayer for the king's justice comes its twin: and your righteousness to the royal son. The good ruler needs more than fair procedures; he needs a rightness of character, and the psalm assumes it must come from God as a gift, not be summoned up by the king himself. Given this righteousness, the son will judge the poor justly and rule as a true king should. The passage does not describe him earning it or growing into it; it simply asks God to hand it down and make it his own. Justice and righteousness together, both received from above, are what mark out a king worth having.
narratives.variation_note: First of five readings of 'righteousness' (H6666, tsedaqah). Here at Psa 72:1 righteousness is a royal endowment received from God, paired with justice. It differs from Psa 106:3 (righteousness constantly practised by the blessed), Psa 106:31 (righteousness reckoned to Phinehas for his zeal), and Psa 112:3 and 112:9 (the God-fearer's enduring righteousness). Here alone it is prayed down into a ruler as the equipment for just government.

narratives.narrative: The sense (101) is 'righteous (tsaddiq) - in his days may the righteous flourish'. Type (102) is status. Source (103) is unrecorded. Seat (104) resolves to none. Bearer (105) is the righteous (inferred). Operation (106) is the core event: they flourish (span-linked, v7). Target (107) is none recorded. Manner (108) is 'with peace abounding' - the flourishing comes wrapped in peace. Intensity (109), specifier (110), effect (111) and prohibition (113) are all absent. Coupling (112) is a span-pairing: the righteous whose flourishing marks the reign (v7). Discovery (114) names them the upright thriving under the just king - righteousness rewarded when the throne is just, their flourishing (and the abundant peace) the fruit of good rule. Role (115) is characteristic; locus (116) is external:person. The full process: with no named source in the self, the righteous flourish as the direct fruit of just government - under a righteous throne the upright thrive and peace spreads; integrity's flourishing is here tied to the justice of the ruler over it.
narratives.story: This is a picture of what a good reign does to good people. Under a king who rules justly, the psalm prays, may the righteous flourish and peace spread as long as the moon lasts. The flourishing of honest people is treated as the natural fruit of just government - when the throne is right, the upright thrive, and peace grows all around them. The passage does not trace this to anything inside the righteous themselves; it ties their thriving to the justice of the ruler above them. Integrity here blossoms in the soil of good rule: give people a just king, and the honest life comes into full flower.
narratives.variation_note: One of seventeen readings of 'righteous' (tsaddiq). Here at Psa 72:7 the righteous flourish specifically as the fruit of a just reign - their thriving tied to the king's justice and wrapped in abundant peace. It differs from the flourishing-images at Psa 92:12 (rooted in God's house) by locating the cause in righteous government rather than in the temple; here integrity's flourishing is a political consequence.

narratives.narrative: The sense (101) is 'pure / clean (bar) - pure in heart'. Type (102) is status: a state of heart-purity. Uniquely for this family, source (103) is present: 'to whom God is good' (span-linked, v1) - the purity is the mark of those God treats well. Seat (104) is the heart (span-linked) - the purity is organ-located, in the heart. Bearer (105) is the pure in heart (inferred). Operation (106) is none recorded - the reading finds no movement; purity here is a settled truth affirmed, not an act. Target (107) is none. Manner (108) is none. Intensity (109), specifier (110), effect (111) and prohibition (113) are all absent. Coupling (112) is a span-pairing: this is the very purity the psalmist thought he had kept in vain (v13). Discovery (114) names it the confessed truth the whole psalm defends against doubt - the creed the psalmist clings to even as his own experience seemed to contradict it. Role (115) is characteristic; locus (116) is internal:ib-state. The full process: with no operation of its own, purity of heart stands as the creed - God is good to the pure in heart - held onto through the crisis of watching the wicked prosper; integrity here is a belief nearly broken by experience and defended anyway.
narratives.story: The psalm begins with a confident creed: truly God is good to those who are pure in heart. But almost at once it wobbles, because the writer looks around and sees the wicked doing wonderfully well while his own clean living seems to get him nothing. So this opening line is not a calm observation - it is a truth he is gripping onto through a storm of doubt. Purity of heart is the mark of the people God is supposed to be good to, and it is the very purity he will later say he kept 'in vain.' The passage sets down the belief at the start, and the whole rest of the psalm is the struggle to keep believing it when experience seems to say otherwise.
narratives.variation_note: Second of two readings of 'pure' (bar). Here at Psa 73:1 purity is the creed the doubting psalmist clings to - a heart-state affirmed as the mark of those God is good to, and notably the only reading in this family with a source recorded (those to whom God is good). It differs from Psa 24:4 (H1249:pure#1), where purity is the entrance-qualification for God's holy hill. There purity opens the way up; here it is the belief that nearly collapsed under the scandal of the wicked's prosperity.

narratives.narrative: The sense (101) is 'keep clean / pure (zakah) - I have kept my heart clean'. Type (102) is action: uniquely, this is a sustained act the self performs on itself. Source (103) is unrecorded. Seat (104) is the heart (span-linked) - the cleanness is worked on the heart. Bearer (105) is the psalmist (inferred). Operation (106) is the core event: keep clean / purify - the self actively maintaining its own heart's purity. Target (107) is 'his heart' (span-linked) - the cleansing is aimed at his own heart. Manner (108) is 'in vain, so it seemed' - the whole labour is coloured by its apparent futility. Intensity (109), specifier (110), effect (111) and prohibition (113) are all absent. Coupling (112) is a span-pairing: keeping the heart clean paired with washing his hands in innocence (v13). Discovery (114) names it the bitter thought that integrity was pointless - the purity he maintained, which the wicked's prosperity made seem wasted; the crisis at its sharpest: why be good if the godless flourish? Role (115) is characteristic; locus (116) is internal:heart. The full process: the psalmist has, by his own sustained effort, kept his heart clean - and now, watching the wicked thrive, he suspects the whole labour was for nothing; integrity read at its point of crisis, self-purity felt as futile.
narratives.story: Here the psalmist looks back on all his hard work at being good - and wonders if it was worth anything. He has kept his heart clean, scrubbed his conduct, washed his hands in innocence, all by real and sustained effort. But the wicked around him are fat, untroubled, rich, and it makes him think: what was the point? All in vain, he says bitterly - I kept myself pure for nothing. This is the crisis at its rawest: the honest person, seeing dishonest people flourish, doubting whether integrity pays at all. The passage does not resolve it here; it simply lets the bitter thought stand - a clean heart that feels, in that moment, like wasted labour.

narratives.narrative: The sense (101) is 'innocence (niqqayon) - washed my hands in innocence'. Type (102) is status: a state of clean-handedness. Source (103) is unrecorded. Seat (104) is the hands (inferred) - the innocence is located in the hands, the organ of deed. Bearer (105) is the psalmist (inferred). Operation (106) is the core event: he washes his hands in innocence. Target (107) is none recorded. Manner (108) is 'in vain, so it seemed' - the innocence, like the clean heart beside it, felt futile. Intensity (109), specifier (110), effect (111) and prohibition (113) are all absent. Coupling (112) is a span-pairing: washing the hands paired with keeping the heart clean (v13). Discovery (114) names it the clean conscience the psalmist maintained - innocence of hands matching the clean heart, purity of act and heart together, which felt wasted beside the wicked's untroubled ease. Role (115) is characteristic; locus (116) is internal:ib-state. The full process: the psalmist has kept his hands innocent as his heart was clean - deed and heart pure together - and now suspects it was all for nothing; integrity's outward side felt as futile as its inward, both shadowed by the prosperity of the godless.
narratives.story: Beside the clean heart stands the clean conscience: I washed my hands in innocence. The psalmist has kept not only his inner life pure but his actions too - no dirty deeds, hands clean. Inside and outside matched. And yet, watching the wicked live at ease and grow rich, he feels the same bitter doubt about his innocent hands as about his clean heart: it all seems wasted. The passage pairs the two - pure heart, pure hands - so that when the crisis hits, it hits the whole of his integrity at once. He kept himself clean in deed as well as in heart, and in that dark moment it looked like it had bought him nothing.

narratives.narrative: The sense (101) is 'righteous (tsaddiq) - the horns of the righteous shall be lifted up'. Type (102) is status. Source (103) is unrecorded. Seat (104) resolves to none. Bearer (105) is the righteous (inferred). Operation (106) is the core event: be lifted up by God (span-linked, v10) - the exalting is God's act. Target (107) is none recorded. Manner (108) is 'horns lifted up, opposite the wicked's cut off' - the exaltation is defined against the wicked's cutting-down. Intensity (109), specifier (110), effect (111) and prohibition (113) are all absent. Coupling (112) is a span-pairing: the righteous set against the wicked whose horns are cut off (v10). Discovery (114) names it the exaltation God grants the upright - the righteous whose horn (strength, dignity) God raises, over against the wicked whose horns he cuts off; the true lifting-up that comes from the Judge, not from self-boasting. Role (115) is characteristic; locus (116) is external:person. The full process: with no source in the self, the righteous are exalted by God - their strength and dignity raised while the boastful wicked, who lifted their own horns, are cut down; integrity's honour is a lifting-up received from the Judge, the opposite of self-exaltation.
narratives.story: The psalm has warned the boastful not to lift up their own horn, their own strength and pride, because real exaltation does not come from the east or west or from tooting your own trumpet - it comes from God, who puts one person down and raises another. Then the contrast lands: God will cut off the horns of the wicked, but the horns of the righteous he will lift up. The honest person does not have to promote himself; the Judge does the lifting. And it is set exactly against the self-promoters, who get cut down. The passage shows integrity's honour as something granted from above - dignity raised by God, not seized by boasting.
narratives.variation_note: One of seventeen readings of 'righteous' (tsaddiq). Here at Psa 75:10 the righteous are exalted by God ('horns lifted up'), defined precisely against the wicked whose horns are cut off and against the self-boasters who lift their own. The distinctive note is the source of honour: exaltation received from the Judge rather than seized, integrity's dignity as a gift from above.

narratives.narrative: The sense (101) is 'be upright (tom)' - 'with upright heart he shepherded them'. Type (102) is disposition: a settled trait of character. Source (103) is unrecorded. Seat (104) resolves to none for the term, though the verse names the heart as the site of the uprightness. Bearer (105) is David (inferred). Operation (106) is the core event: be upright / of integrity - David's character in the act of shepherding. Target (107) is 'in shepherding the people' (inferred) - the integrity is exercised in leadership. Manner (108) is none. Intensity (109), specifier (110), effect (111) and prohibition (113) are all absent. Coupling (112) is the upright heart paired with the skilful hand (inferred) - integrity of heart joined to competence of hand. Discovery (114) names it the integrity of the shepherd-king, the psalm's counter to the faithless generation it has just rehearsed. Role (115) is characteristic; locus (116) is internal:ib-state. The full process: from no named source, David shepherds the people out of an upright heart, integrity guiding the exercise of leadership and joined to a skilful hand; character read as the inner quality that makes a leader trustworthy, set against a whole generation that was not.
narratives.story: After a long, painful memory of a whole nation that kept betraying God, the psalm ends on one bright figure: David, taken from tending sheep to shepherd God's people. And the thing it praises in him is not his cleverness or his crown but the quality of his heart - with an upright heart he shepherded them, and guided them with a skilful hand. Integrity of heart paired with competence of hand: that is what makes a leader you can trust. Set against a faithless generation, David stands out precisely because his inner life was whole. The passage shows uprightness as the deep character that makes leadership honest - the heart behind the hand.

narratives.narrative: The sense (101) is 'weak (dal)'. Type (102) is status: the weak as a powerless standing. Source (103) is unrecorded. Seat (104) resolves to none. Bearer (105) is the weak (inferred) - the powerless whose cause the judges should uphold. Operation (106) is the core event: be denied justice - the weak are those the corrupt bench neglects. Target (107) is 'by the judges' (inferred) - the neglect comes from those charged to judge. Manner (108) is none. Intensity (109), specifier (110), effect (111) and prohibition (113) are all absent. Coupling (112) is the weak paired with the fatherless (inferred). Discovery (114) sets it at v3: 'give justice to the weak and the fatherless' - the powerless whose cause the judges neglect; their helpless state indicts the bench. Role (115) is characteristic; locus (116) is internal:ib-state. The full process: with no source in themselves, the weak stand as those to whom justice is owed and denied - their very helplessness the measure of the judges' failure; integrity is read here from its victims' side, the powerless whose neglected cause exposes a corrupt bench. Note the reading holds 'weak' among the righteousness-integrity terms not as a virtue but as the object justice exists to protect.
narratives.story: God stands up in the divine council and indicts the judges: how long will you side with the wicked and ignore the helpless? Then he names who they are supposed to protect - the weak, the fatherless. These are people with no power to defend themselves, and their whole plight is a mirror held up to the judges' failure. Justice exists precisely to shield them, and the judges have withheld it. The passage does not treat weakness as a virtue; it treats the weak as the test of whether justice is real. Where the powerless are denied, the whole system of judgment stands condemned. Their helplessness is the evidence against the bench.
narratives.variation_note: First of two readings of 'weak' (dal). Here at Psa 82:3 the weak are those denied justice by the corrupt judges - the neglect coming from the bench that should defend them. At Psa 82:4 (H1800:weak#2) the same word names the weak who need rescue from the hand of the wicked. The difference: v3 is about justice withheld by the judges (neglect), v4 about deliverance needed from active predators (assault) - the powerless failed in two ways, by those who should help and by those who prey.

narratives.narrative: The sense (101) is 'weak (dal)'. Type (102) is status. Source (103) is unrecorded. Seat (104) resolves to none. Bearer (105) is the weak (inferred). Operation (106) is the core event: need rescue - the weak as those who must be delivered. Target (107) is 'from the wicked' (inferred) - the danger is the wicked's hand. Manner (108) is none. Intensity (109), specifier (110), effect (111) and prohibition (113) are all absent. Coupling (112) is the weak paired with the needy (inferred). Discovery (114) sets it at v4: 'rescue the weak and the needy' - the powerless again named as those the judges should but do not defend. Role (115) is characteristic; locus (116) is internal:ib-state. The full process: with no source in themselves, the weak stand as those needing deliverance from the wicked's grip - the justice owed them is not only a fair hearing but active rescue; integrity read from the side of those it must protect, the powerless in the hand of predators.
narratives.story: The charge to the judges sharpens: rescue the weak and the needy; deliver them from the hand of the wicked. It is not enough to give them a fair hearing in court - they need to be actively pulled out of the grip of those preying on them. The weak here are people in real danger from the strong, and justice means stepping in to save them. The passage keeps the lens on the powerless and what is owed them: not just fairness but rescue. Where the judges fail to snatch the helpless out of the predator's hand, they betray the whole reason they hold the bench.
narratives.variation_note: Second of two readings of 'weak' (dal). Here at Psa 82:4 the weak need active rescue from the hand of the wicked - deliverance from predators. It differs from Psa 82:3 (H1800:weak#1), where the weak are denied justice by the judges themselves. Together they show the powerless failed twice over: neglected by the bench that should judge for them (v3) and menaced by the wicked they must be saved from (v4).

narratives.narrative: The sense (101) is 'uprightly (tamim)' - 'those who walk uprightly'. Type (102) is disposition: a settled character of blamelessness. Source (103) is unrecorded. Seat (104) resolves to none. Bearer (105) is the upright (inferred). Operation (106) is the core event: be blameless - integrity as the shape of the walk.
