Target (107) is 'in walk' (inferred) - the blamelessness is worked out in the God-ward life. Manner (108) is none. Intensity (109), specifier (110), effect (111) and prohibition (113) are all absent. Coupling (112) is the uprightness paired with the walking (inferred). Discovery (114) sets it at v11: 'from those who walk uprightly' - the integrity of the God-ward life, blamelessness as the pilgrim's character. Role (115) is characteristic; locus (116) is internal:ib-state. The full process: from no named source, the pilgrim who longs for God's courts walks in blamelessness, and to such a one God withholds no good thing; integrity read as the settled uprightness of a life oriented toward God, the character of the one who dwells in his house.
narratives.story: The whole psalm aches to be near God - the writer envies the sparrows nesting by the altar and would rather be a doorkeeper in God's house than live anywhere else. And at the end it makes a promise about who receives God's good: no good thing does he withhold from those who walk uprightly. Blamelessness here is the settled character of the pilgrim, the shape of a life turned toward God. It is not a single act but a way of walking. The passage ties God's open-handed generosity to this integrity of life: to the one who lives whole and honest before God, nothing good is denied.

narratives.narrative: The sense (101) is 'righteous (tsaddiq)'. Type (102) is status. Source (103) is unrecorded. Seat (104) resolves to none. Bearer (105) is the righteous (inferred). Operation (106) is the core event: flourish like a palm - lasting, fruitful growth. Target (107) is 'planted in God's house' (inferred) - the flourishing is rooted in God's dwelling. Manner (108) is none. Intensity (109), specifier (110), effect (111) and prohibition (113) are all absent. Coupling (112) as recorded reads 'internal:ib-state' - the reading binds the flourishing into an inner condition; and locus (116) pairs it with growing like a cedar (v12). Discovery (114) sets it at v12: 'the righteous flourish like the palm tree' - the upright whose God-rooted life bears lasting fruit, set against the grass-like wicked who spring up and are doomed. Role (115) is characteristic. The full process: with no named source in the self, the righteous flourish like palm and cedar - deep-rooted, long-lived, fruitful - because they are planted in God's house; integrity's growth is slow, permanent, and God-rooted, the exact opposite of the wicked who sprout like grass only to be destroyed.
narratives.story: Two kinds of growth are set against each other. The wicked sprout up fast like grass - lush for a moment, then gone, doomed to destruction. The righteous grow differently: like a palm tree, like a cedar of Lebanon - slow, deep-rooted, long-lived, still bearing fruit in old age. And the secret is where they are planted: in the house of God. Their flourishing is not a quick burst but a permanent, God-rooted thriving. The passage draws the contrast to make a point about integrity - the honest life may not shoot up overnight, but it stands for generations, green and fruitful, because its roots are in God.
narratives.variation_note: One of seventeen readings of 'righteous' (tsaddiq). Here at Psa 92:12 the righteous flourish like palm and cedar - deep-rooted in God's house, set against the grass-like wicked. It differs from Psa 72:7, where the righteous flourish as the fruit of a just reign; there the cause is good government, here it is being planted in God's dwelling. Integrity's flourishing is grounded in the temple rather than the throne.

narratives.narrative: The sense (101) is 'upright (yashar)'. Type (102) is status. Source (103) is unrecorded. Seat (104) resolves to none. Bearer (105) is the upright (inferred). Operation (106) is the core event: follow justice - the upright pursue the justice that returns. Target (107) is 'after God' (inferred) - the following is Godward, aligned with his verdict. Manner (108) is none. Intensity (109), specifier (110), effect (111) and prohibition (113) are all absent. Coupling (112) is the upright paired with the upright heart (inferred). Discovery (114) sets it at v15: 'all the upright in heart will follow it' - the upright who pursue the returning justice, aligned with God's verdict. Role (115) is characteristic; locus (116) is internal:ib-state. The full process: from no named source, when justice returns to the righteous, the upright in heart fall in behind it - actively following, their inner rectitude drawing them after God's restored verdict; integrity read as a heart that moves toward justice once God re-establishes it.
narratives.story: The psalm promises that justice, which had seemed to vanish under wicked rulers who 'frame injustice by statute,' will come back around to the righteous. And when it does, the upright do not just receive it passively - they follow it. All the upright in heart will fall in behind the returning justice, moving after it, aligned with God's restored verdict. Their honesty shows itself as a kind of magnetism toward what is right: when God sets justice back on its feet, the straight-hearted are drawn after it. The passage pictures integrity not as standing still but as a heart that goes where justice goes, once God brings it home.
narratives.variation_note: Fourth of ten readings of 'upright' (yashar). Here at Psa 94:15 the upright actively follow returning justice - a movement toward God's restored verdict. It is distinct among the yashar readings for making the upright pursuers of justice rather than recipients of reward or rejoicers at judgment; integrity here is a heart that moves after what is right.

narratives.narrative: The sense (101) is 'righteous (tsedeq)'. Type (102) is status. Source (103) is unrecorded. Seat (104) resolves to none. Bearer (105) is the righteous (inferred). Operation (106) is the core event: receive justice - justice returns to the righteous. Target (107) is 'from God' (inferred) - the justice comes from God. Manner (108) is none. Intensity (109), specifier (110), effect (111) and prohibition (113) are all absent. Coupling (112) as recorded reads 'internal:ib-state'; locus (116) pairs the righteous with the upright in heart (v15). Discovery (114) sets it at v15: 'for justice will return to the righteous' - the righteous to whom judgment will come back round, vindication assured. Role (115) is characteristic. The full process: with no source in the self, the righteous are those to whom justice returns - after a season when wicked rulers twisted the law, God's verdict swings back to the upright; integrity read as the party to whom justice is owed and will be restored, paired with the upright hearts who then follow it.
narratives.story: For a while in this psalm the law itself has been hijacked - wicked rulers dressing up injustice as legal statute, banding together to condemn the innocent. But the promise is that this cannot last: justice will return to the righteous. The verdict that had been stolen swings back to the honest, and God sees to it. The righteous are the ones to whom justice is owed, and it will find its way home to them. The passage pairs them with all the upright in heart who then follow that justice. Integrity here is vindicated by patience - the honest wait, and the moral order comes back around to them.
narratives.variation_note: This 'righteous' at Psa 94:15 is tsedeq (H6664), sharing the verse with the yashar 'upright' reading. Here the righteous receive returning justice (they are its destination); the paired yashar reading has the upright actively follow it. The two halves of the verse split the movement: justice comes back to the righteous, and the upright then fall in behind it - the party owed and the party in pursuit.

narratives.narrative: The sense (101) is 'innocent (naqi)'. Type (102) is status: the innocent as a guiltless standing. Source (103) is unrecorded. Seat (104) resolves to none. Bearer (105) is the innocent (inferred). Operation (106) is the core event: be condemned - the guiltless sentenced. Target (107) is 'by the wicked' (inferred) - the condemnation comes from wicked rulers. Manner (108) is none. Intensity (109), specifier (110), effect (111) and prohibition (113) are all absent. Coupling (112) as recorded reads 'internal:ib-state'; locus (116) pairs the innocent with the act of condemning (v21). Discovery (114) sets it at v21: 'and condemn the innocent to death' - the guiltless victim, whose very innocence the wicked assail. Role (115) is characteristic. The full process: with no source in themselves, the innocent stand as those the wicked rulers band together to condemn and kill - their guiltlessness no protection but the very thing assailed; integrity read from its victim's side, the blameless sentenced to death by those who 'frame injustice by statute'.
narratives.story: The wicked rulers in this psalm do not just bend the law - they use it to kill. They band together against the life of the righteous and condemn the innocent to death. Here is integrity under its worst assault: a guiltless person, and their innocence buys them nothing, because the very people meant to protect them are the ones handing down the death sentence. The passage does not pretend that being innocent keeps you safe. It shows the blameless targeted precisely by a corrupted justice, condemned by statute-dressed wickedness. It is the dark side of the same story that promises justice will return - first, the innocent suffer at the hands of those who should have defended them.

narratives.narrative: The sense (101) is 'upright (yashar)' - 'joy for the upright in heart'. Type (102) is status. Source (103) is unrecorded. Seat (104) resolves to none for the term, though the verse names the heart. Bearer (105) is the upright (inferred). Operation (106) is the core event: be upright - here the upright as those for whom joy is stored. Target (107) is 'in heart' (inferred). Manner (108) is none. Intensity (109), specifier (110), effect (111) and prohibition (113) are all absent. Coupling (112) as recorded reads 'internal:ib-state'; locus (116) pairs the upright with the joy sown for them (v11). Discovery (114) sets it at v11: 'joy for the upright in heart' - the straight-hearted for whom joy is stored. Role (115) is characteristic. The full process: with no named source, the upright in heart are those for whom joy is sown and kept - as light is sown for the righteous, joy is laid up for the straight of heart; integrity read as the condition to which God assigns a coming harvest of gladness.
narratives.story: The psalm uses a farming image for what God stores up for good people: light is sown for the righteous, and joy for the upright in heart. Sown - like seed put in the ground, promising a harvest still to come. The straight-hearted may not see the gladness yet, but it is planted for them, waiting to spring up. Integrity here is the kind of heart to which God assigns a future full of joy. The passage does not spell out when or how; it simply promises that the honest heart has gladness seeded for it, ripening ahead. What is coming for the upright is light and joy, already in the ground.
narratives.variation_note: Fifth of ten readings of 'upright' (yashar), sharing Psa 97:11 with the tsaddiq reading. Here the upright in heart have joy 'sown' for them - a stored, future gladness, paralleling the light sown for the righteous in the same verse. The distinctive image is the agricultural 'sowing': integrity's reward as a planted harvest, not yet reaped.

narratives.narrative: The sense (101) is 'righteous (tsaddiq)' - 'light is sown for the righteous'. Type (102) is status. Source (103) is unrecorded. Seat (104) resolves to none. Bearer (105) is the righteous (inferred). Operation (106) is the core event: have light sown - light stored up for them. Target (107) is 'for them' (inferred). Manner (108) is none. Intensity (109), specifier (110), effect (111) and prohibition (113) are all absent. Coupling (112) as recorded reads 'internal:ib-state'; locus (116) pairs the righteous with the joy for the upright (v11). Discovery (114) sets it at v11: 'light is sown for the righteous' - the just for whom God stores up light, brightness appointed the upright. Role (115) is characteristic. The full process: with no source in the self, the righteous are those for whom light is sown - a coming brightness planted and kept for them, paired with the joy sown for the upright; integrity read as the condition to which God assigns a harvest of light, even when the present is dark.
narratives.story: Right after the psalm warns that God delivers his people from the hand of the wicked, it drops a quiet promise: light is sown for the righteous. Light - like seed - planted for the honest, waiting to break the surface. The image says the brightness may not be visible now, but it is in the ground, guaranteed, growing toward them. Paired with the joy sown for the upright, it tells the righteous that a harvest of light and gladness is coming, whatever the present darkness. Integrity does not always feel luminous in the moment; but for the just, the psalm says, light is already planted, and it will surely rise.
narratives.variation_note: One of seventeen readings of 'righteous' (tsaddiq), sharing Psa 97:11 with the yashar reading. Here light is 'sown' for the righteous - the same agricultural image of a planted, future harvest. It differs from the many tsaddiq readings of received joy or rescue by stressing the not-yet, seeded quality of the reward: light guaranteed but still growing toward the just.

narratives.narrative: The sense (101) is 'righteous (tsaddiq)' - 'Rejoice in the LORD, O you righteous'. Type (102) is status. Source (103) is unrecorded. Seat (104) resolves to none. Bearer (105) is the righteous (inferred). Operation (106) is the core event: rejoice - the just called to joy. Target (107) is 'in God' (inferred) - the joy is directed to the LORD. Manner (108) is none. Intensity (109), specifier (110), effect (111) and prohibition (113) are all absent. Coupling (112) as recorded reads 'internal:ib-state'; locus (116) pairs the righteous with the rejoicing itself (v12). Discovery (114) sets it at v12: 'Rejoice in the LORD, O you righteous' - the just called to joy and thanks. Role (115) is characteristic. The full process: with no named source, the righteous are summoned to rejoice in the LORD and give thanks to his holy name - integrity read here not as a reward received but as a called response; the just are commanded into joy, their proper answer to the God who stores light and gladness for them.
narratives.story: Having promised that light and joy are sown for the honest, the psalm turns and gives them a command: rejoice in the Lord, you righteous, and give thanks to his holy name. This is not a reward handed over so much as a summons issued. The upright are called to respond to their God with joy and gratitude. Integrity here is asked to answer - to lift its voice and be glad in the Lord who is setting the world right. The passage closes by turning the righteous from recipients into worshippers: given a God who stores up brightness for them, the fitting thing to do is rejoice and give thanks.
narratives.variation_note: One of seventeen readings of 'righteous' (tsaddiq), the second in Psa 97 (with #10 at v11). Here at v12 the righteous are commanded to rejoice - a called response, where v11 had them receiving sown light. The pair moves from gift to summons: light stored for the just (v11), then the just summoned to answer with joy and thanks (v12).

narratives.narrative: The sense (101) is 'integrity (tom)' - 'I will walk with integrity of heart'. Type (102) is disposition: a settled resolve of character. Source (103) is unrecorded. Seat (104) resolves to none for the term, though the verse names the heart. Bearer (105) is David (inferred). Operation (106) is the core event: have integrity of heart - the king resolving to live with an undivided moral purpose. Target (107) is 'of heart' (inferred) - the integrity is heart-deep. Manner (108) is none. Intensity (109), specifier (110), effect (111) and prohibition (113) are all absent. Coupling (112) as recorded reads 'internal:ib-state'; locus (116) pairs the integrity with the walking and the heart (v2). Discovery (114) sets it at v2: 'I will walk with integrity of heart' - the wholeness of moral purpose, the king's undivided commitment. Role (115) is characteristic. The full process: from no named source, David resolves to walk with an undivided heart within his own house - integrity read as a forward-looking commitment to wholeness of purpose, the private resolve that grounds a whole psalm of public governance (whom he will admit, whom he will destroy).
narratives.story: This is a king making a private vow before he ever talks about governing. I will walk with integrity of heart within my own house - the resolve to be whole, undivided, the same person behind closed doors as in public. Everything else in the psalm - who he will welcome, who he will not tolerate, the liars he will banish - grows out of this first commitment to his own inner honesty. Integrity here is a chosen direction, a purpose set for the future: to keep his heart single and true. The passage roots public justice in private wholeness. Before he cleans up the kingdom, the king pledges to keep his own heart clean.
narratives.variation_note: Fourth of four readings of 'integrity' (tom). Here at Psa 101:2 integrity is a forward resolve - David's chosen commitment to walk whole-heartedly. It differs from Psa 7:8 (integrity offered to God's judgment), Psa 25:21 (integrity pleaded as a preserver), and Psa 41:12 (integrity gratefully seen already honoured). Here alone integrity is future-facing resolve, the private wholeness that grounds a psalm about public rule.

narratives.narrative: The sense (101) is 'blameless (tamim)' - 'I will ponder the way that is blameless'. Type (102) is disposition. Source (103) is unrecorded. Seat (104) resolves to none. Bearer (105) is David (inferred). Operation (106) is the core event: pursue the blameless way - to ponder and set it before himself. Target (107) is 'before God' (inferred). Manner (108) is none. Intensity (109), specifier (110), effect (111) and prohibition (113) are all absent. Coupling (112) as recorded reads 'internal:ib-state'; locus (116) pairs the blamelessness with the pondering of it (v2). Discovery (114) sets it at v2: 'I will ponder the way that is blameless' - the whole, undivided way of life David sets before himself. Role (115) is characteristic. The full process: from no named source, David studies and sets his mind on the blameless way - integrity read as a deliberate attention, the way of wholeness taken up as an object of thought and intention before it is walked; the resolve of a king to fix his gaze on a life without fault.
narratives.story: Alongside his vow to walk with an undivided heart, the king does something quieter: he studies the blameless way. I will ponder the way that is blameless - he sets his mind on it, thinks it over, keeps it in view. Integrity is not just lived here but considered, made an object of attention. Before he walks it, he fixes his gaze on what a faultless life would look like. The passage shows that being blameless starts as a deliberate act of thought - choosing to keep the whole, undivided way in front of you, turning it over, intending it. The king's uprightness begins in where he decides to point his mind.
narratives.variation_note: Second of five readings of 'blameless' (tamim), sharing Psa 101:2 with the integrity reading. Here blamelessness is pondered and resolved on - a way of life set before the mind. It differs from Psa 18:23 (blamelessness as active self-guarding), Psa 101:6 (blamelessness as the standard for others), Psa 119:1 (blamelessness pronounced blessed), and Psa 119:80 (blamelessness of heart pleaded for). Here alone it is an object of deliberate contemplation.

narratives.narrative: The sense (101) is 'blameless (tamim)' - 'he who walks in the way that is blameless'. Type (102) is disposition. Source (103) is unrecorded. Seat (104) resolves to none. Bearer (105) is the servant (inferred) - not the king himself here but the one who would serve him. Operation (106) is the core event: be blameless - the integrity that qualifies for the king's household. Target (107) is 'in the way' (inferred). Manner (108) is none. Intensity (109), specifier (110), effect (111) and prohibition (113) are all absent. Coupling (112) as recorded reads 'internal:ib-state'; locus (116) pairs the blamelessness with walking (v6). Discovery (114) sets it at v6: 'he who walks in the way that is blameless shall minister to me' - the integrity that qualifies for the king's household. Role (115) is characteristic. The full process: from no named source, blamelessness becomes the criterion the king applies to others - the one who walks the whole, faultless way is the one admitted to serve him; integrity read outward, as the standard by which the king sorts those who may be near him, the same wholeness he vowed for himself now required of his servants.
narratives.story: Having pledged his own integrity, the king turns it into a hiring policy. The one who walks the blameless way, he says, is the one who gets to serve me. Blamelessness here is not just his private commitment but the standard he holds others to - the test for who is allowed into his household and his service. Liars and the deceitful are shown the door; the faithful and whole-living are welcomed close. The passage shows integrity working outward: the same wholeness the king wants in himself, he now requires in the people around him. Character becomes the qualification. To be near this king, you have to walk the faultless way.
narratives.variation_note: Third of five readings of 'blameless' (tamim). Here at Psa 101:6 blamelessness is the criterion the king applies to others - the standard for who may serve him. It differs from the readings where blamelessness is the self's own (18:23 self-guarding, 101:2 resolved on, 119:80 pleaded for) by turning integrity outward into a test applied to servants. The king's private wholeness becomes a public requirement.

narratives.narrative: The sense (101) is 'justice (mishpat)' - 'they who observe justice'. Type (102) is disposition: a settled habit of just dealing. Source (103) is unrecorded. Seat (104) resolves to none. Bearer (105) is the just (inferred) - those pronounced blessed. Operation (106) is the core event: keep justice - to observe it steadily. Target (107) is 'at all times' (inferred) - the justice is constant, not occasional. Manner (108) is none. Intensity (109), specifier (110), effect (111) and prohibition (113) are all absent. Coupling (112) as recorded reads 'internal:ib-state'; locus (116) pairs justice with righteousness (v3). Discovery (114) sets it at v3: 'they who observe justice' - the justice the blessed keep, righteous dealing. Role (115) is characteristic. The full process: from no named source, the blessed are those who keep justice constantly - integrity read as a sustained habit, justice not done once but observed at all times; the ideal against which the psalm will confess Israel's long history of failure, righteousness held up as the mark of the truly blessed.
narratives.story: The psalm opens its long, painful confession of national failure with a picture of the opposite - the blessed life. Blessed are they who observe justice, who do what is right at all times. The key words are 'at all times': justice here is not an occasional good deed but a steady, unbroken habit, woven through the whole of life. This is the standard, held up bright, before the psalm admits that both the fathers and the present generation fell far short of it. The passage makes justice the mark of a blessed person - not a single fair act, but the constant practice of fair dealing, right conduct kept up all the time.
narratives.variation_note: Second of three readings of 'justice' (mishpat), paired with righteousness in the same verse. Here at Psa 106:3 justice is a constant habit of the blessed ('at all times'). It differs from Psa 72:1 (justice as a governing gift prayed into the king) and Psa 112:5 (justice in a man's private business dealings). Here alone justice is framed as the sustained practice that defines the blessed, the ideal against which Israel's failures are confessed.

narratives.narrative: The sense (101) is 'righteousness (tsedaqah)' - 'who do righteousness at all times'. Type (102) is disposition. Source (103) is unrecorded. Seat (104) resolves to none. Bearer (105) is the just (inferred). Operation (106) is the core event: do righteousness - to practise it. Target (107) is 'at all times' (inferred) - constant, unbroken. Manner (108) is none. Intensity (109), specifier (110), effect (111) and prohibition (113) are all absent. Coupling (112) as recorded reads 'internal:ib-state'; locus (116) pairs righteousness with justice (v3). Discovery (114) sets it at v3: 'who do righteousness at all times!' - the constant right conduct of the blessed, the ideal against which Israel's history is confessed. Role (115) is characteristic. The full process: from no named source, the blessed are those who do righteousness constantly - integrity read as unbroken right conduct, paired with the keeping of justice; together they form the standard the psalm sets up before rehearsing a history of sin, righteousness as the sustained doing that marks the truly blessed.
narratives.story: Beside the constant keeping of justice stands its twin: who do righteousness at all times. Again the weight falls on 'at all times' - right conduct that never clocks off, a steady doing of good woven through every hour. The two together, justice and righteousness kept constantly, paint the portrait of the blessed life. And the psalm holds this bright ideal up precisely so that the long confession that follows - we and our fathers have sinned - lands with full force. The passage makes righteousness a matter of unbroken practice, not occasional virtue: the mark of a truly blessed person is doing what is right, all the time, without letting up.
narratives.variation_note: Second of five readings of 'righteousness' (H6666, tsedaqah), paired with justice in the same verse. Here at Psa 106:3 righteousness is constant practice ('at all times'). It differs from Psa 72:1 (righteousness as a royal endowment), Psa 106:31 (righteousness reckoned to Phinehas for a single act of zeal), and Psa 112:3/9 (the God-fearer's enduring righteousness). Here it is the sustained doing that defines the blessed, set against the nation's confessed failures.

narratives.narrative: The sense (101) is 'righteousness (tsedaqah)' - 'that was counted to him as righteousness'. Type (102) is state: righteousness here as a reckoned status. Source (103) is unrecorded. Seat (104) resolves to none. Bearer (105) is Phinehas (inferred). Operation (106) is the core event: be counted righteous - his zealous act reckoned to his credit. Target (107) is 'for his zeal' (inferred) - the righteousness is credited for his intervention. Manner (108) is none. Intensity (109), specifier (110), effect (111) and prohibition (113) are all absent. Coupling (112) as recorded reads 'internal:ib-state'; locus (116) pairs the righteousness with his intervention (v31). Discovery (114) sets it at v31: 'and that was counted to him as righteousness' - the reckoning of Phinehas' zeal to his everlasting credit. Role (115) is characteristic. The full process: with no named source, a single decisive act - Phinehas standing up to halt the plague - is counted to him as righteousness from generation to generation; integrity read here as an imputed reckoning, a status credited for one deed of zeal and made permanent, distinct from the sustained-practice righteousness of v3.
narratives.story: In the middle of a grim catalogue of Israel's rebellions, one man stands out. A plague is raging as punishment for the people's sin, and Phinehas steps in, intervenes, and the plague stops. And the psalm says something remarkable about it: that act was counted to him as righteousness, from generation to generation, forever. Here righteousness is not a lifelong habit but a reckoning - one decisive deed of zeal credited to a man's account and made permanent. God took his intervention and wrote it down as righteousness that would never expire. The passage shows integrity in a different key: not the slow accumulation of right living, but a single brave act reckoned to lasting credit.
narratives.variation_note: Third of five readings of 'righteousness' (H6666, tsedaqah), and the most distinctive: here at Psa 106:31 righteousness is reckoned/imputed to Phinehas for a single act of zeal - a state credited and made everlasting. It differs sharply from the sustained-practice readings (106:3 'at all times', 112:3/9 'endures forever') and from the royal endowment (72:1). This alone reads righteousness as a status counted for one decisive deed rather than a habit or gift.

narratives.narrative: The sense (101) is 'upright (yashar)' - 'the upright see it and are glad'. Type (102) is status. Source (103) is unrecorded. Seat (104) resolves to none. Bearer (105) is the upright (inferred). Operation (106) is the core event: see and be glad - at God's reversals. Target (107) is 'at God's reversals' (inferred) - the raising of the needy, the humbling of princes. Manner (108) is none. Intensity (109), specifier (110), effect (111) and prohibition (113) are all absent. Coupling (112) as recorded reads 'internal:ib-state'; locus (116) pairs the upright with their being glad (v42). Discovery (114) sets it at v42: 'the upright see it and are glad' - the just who rejoice to see God set things right. Role (115) is characteristic. The full process: with no named source, the upright watch God overturn the order - pouring contempt on princes, raising the needy from affliction - and are glad; integrity read as a heart that delights when God reverses injustice, its gladness set against the wickedness that, in the same verse, shuts its mouth.
narratives.story: The psalm has just described God turning the world the right way up - humbling arrogant princes and sending them to wander in wastelands, while lifting the poor out of misery and making their families flourish like flocks. And when the upright see this, they are glad. Their gladness is the natural response of an honest heart to seeing God set things right, to watching the powerful brought low and the helpless raised. In the same breath, wickedness shuts its mouth - it has nothing to say. The passage pairs the two reactions: the upright rejoice, the wicked fall silent. Integrity delights to see justice done; corruption can only look on, speechless.
narratives.variation_note: Sixth of ten readings of 'upright' (yashar). Here at Psa 107:42 the upright see God's reversals and are glad, their joy set against the silenced wicked. It shares the 'see and rejoice at God's justice' motif with the tsaddiq readings (58:10, 64:10) but focuses on God's social reversals - princes humbled, the needy raised - as the specific occasion of the upright's gladness.

narratives.narrative: The sense (101) is 'upright (yashar)' - 'in the company of the upright'. Type (102) is status. Source (103) is unrecorded. Seat (104) resolves to none. Bearer (105) is the upright (inferred). Operation (106) is the core event: gather - the upright as an assembled fellowship. Target (107) is 'to praise God' (inferred) - the gathering is for thanksgiving. Manner (108) is none. Intensity (109), specifier (110), effect (111) and prohibition (113) are all absent. Coupling (112) as recorded reads 'internal:ib-state'; locus (116) pairs the upright with the thanksgiving in the assembly (v1). Discovery (114) sets it at v1: 'in the company of the upright, in the congregation' - the righteous among whom the psalmist gives thanks, the fellowship of the godly. Role (115) is characteristic. The full process: with no named source, the upright form the gathered company in which the psalmist gives whole-hearted thanks - integrity read here as a communal reality, the fellowship of the godly assembled to praise; uprightness located not only in the single heart but in the congregation the honest keep.
narratives.story: The psalmist does not give thanks alone. I will give thanks to the Lord with my whole heart, he says - in the company of the upright, in the congregation. Here integrity shows up as fellowship: the upright are a gathered people, an assembly of the honest among whom praise is offered. Being upright is not only a private quality but a shared one, marked by the company you keep and the congregation you join. The passage locates the honest heart within a community of other honest hearts, all assembled to thank God together. Integrity, on this reading, has a social side - it gathers, it belongs, it praises in company.
narratives.variation_note: Seventh of ten readings of 'upright' (yashar). Here at Psa 111:1 the upright are a gathered congregation - a fellowship of the godly in which thanks is offered. It is distinctive for reading uprightness communally rather than individually: integrity as the company the honest keep, not just a trait of the single heart. Most yashar readings focus on the individual upright; this one names their assembly.

narratives.narrative: The sense (101) is 'upright (yashar)' - 'the generation of the upright will be blessed'. Type (102) is status. Source (103) is unrecorded. Seat (104) resolves to none. Bearer (105) is the upright (inferred). Operation (106) is the core event: be blessed - as a whole generation. Target (107) is 'as a generation' (inferred) - the blessing falls on their line. Manner (108) is none. Intensity (109), specifier (110), effect (111) and prohibition (113) are all absent. Coupling (112) as recorded reads 'internal:ib-state'; locus (116) pairs the upright with the blessing on their line (v2). Discovery (114) sets it at v2: 'the generation of the upright will be blessed' - the upright whose very line is blessed. Role (115) is characteristic. The full process: with no named source, the upright are blessed not only in themselves but in their descendants - their offspring mighty in the land, their whole generation blessed; integrity read as a good that outruns the individual, spilling forward into the line that comes after the honest.
narratives.story: The blessing of an upright life does not stop with the person who lives it. His children will be mighty in the land, the psalm says, and the whole generation of the upright will be blessed. Integrity here has a forward reach: the honest person's uprightness spills over onto the family that follows, so that his line inherits the good he sowed. The passage widens the frame from the individual to the generation - being upright is not just a private benefit but a legacy handed down. The good of a whole-hearted life outruns the one who lived it, blessing the children and the children's children who come after.
narratives.variation_note: Eighth of ten readings of 'upright' (yashar). Here at Psa 112:2 the upright are blessed as a whole generation - the blessing reaching their descendants. It is distinctive for its generational scope: where other yashar readings bless or reward the individual upright, this one extends the good forward onto the line. Integrity as inheritance.

narratives.narrative: The sense (101) is 'righteousness (tsedaqah)' - 'his righteousness endures forever'. Type (102) is disposition. Source (103) is unrecorded. Seat (104) resolves to none. Bearer (105) is the man - the God-fearer (inferred). Operation (106) is the core event: be righteous - enduringly. Target (107) is 'enduringly' (inferred) - the righteousness lasts. Manner (108) is none. Intensity (109), specifier (110), effect (111) and prohibition (113) are all absent. Coupling (112) as recorded reads 'internal:ib-state'; locus (116) pairs it with the enduring of his righteousness (v3). Discovery (114) sets it at v3: 'and his righteousness endures forever' - the lasting rightness of the God-fearer, righteousness that outlasts wealth. Role (115) is characteristic. The full process: with no named source, the God-fearer's righteousness endures forever - set in the same verse beside wealth and riches in his house, it is the possession that lasts when riches do not; integrity read as a permanent quality, the rightness that outlives everything else a person holds.
narratives.story: The psalm lists what the God-fearing man has - wealth and riches in his house - and then, in the same breath, names the one thing that outlasts all of it: his righteousness endures forever. Money comes and goes; the rightness of his life does not. Integrity here is the permanent possession, the thing that stays when everything else is spent. The passage sets the two side by side deliberately: riches that fill a house today, and a righteousness that stands forever. Of the two, only one is truly his to keep. The honest life, on this reading, is the one investment that never loses its value - it endures when the wealth around it fades.
narratives.variation_note: Fourth of five readings of 'righteousness' (H6666, tsedaqah). Here at Psa 112:3 righteousness is the God-fearer's enduring quality, set against transient wealth. It differs from Psa 72:1 (royal endowment) and Psa 106:31 (a reckoned status for one act), and pairs closely with Psa 112:9 (righteousness enduring in generosity) in the same psalm. Here the accent is permanence against riches; at v9 it is permanence expressed in giving.

narratives.narrative: The sense (101) is 'upright (yashar)' - 'light dawns in the darkness for the upright'. Type (102) is status. Source (103) is unrecorded. Seat (104) resolves to none. Bearer (105) is the upright (inferred). Operation (106) is the core event: be given light - light rising for them in the dark. Target (107) is 'in darkness' (inferred) - the light comes precisely in the dark. Manner (108) is none. Intensity (109), specifier (110), effect (111) and prohibition (113) are all absent. Coupling (112) as recorded reads 'internal:ib-state'; locus (116) pairs the upright with the light that dawns for them (v4). Discovery (114) sets it at v4: 'Light dawns in the darkness for the upright' - the upright for whom light rises even in the dark. Role (115) is characteristic. The full process: with no named source, the upright receive light dawning in their darkness - integrity read as the condition to which God sends light at the darkest point; the honest are not spared darkness but met within it by a dawning brightness, hope breaking precisely where it is dark.
narratives.story: This is not a promise that the upright never see darkness - it is better than that. Light dawns in the darkness for the upright. The honest do pass through dark times; the difference is that light breaks in on them there, right in the middle of the gloom. Dawn comes precisely where it is darkest. Integrity does not buy a life without trouble, but it is met by a rising light when trouble comes. The passage pictures the upright person in the dark and then a sunrise breaking over them. Whatever the darkness, the straight-hearted can count on light coming to find them in it - hope dawning exactly where it is needed.
narratives.variation_note: Ninth of ten readings of 'upright' (yashar), sharing Psa 112:4 with a tsaddiq reading. Here light dawns for the upright specifically in darkness - the distinctive note being that the reward meets them in trouble rather than replacing it. Where other yashar readings promise blessing or joy, this one promises light within the dark, hope at the low point.

narratives.narrative: The sense (101) is 'righteous (tsaddiq)' - 'gracious, merciful, and righteous'. Type (102) is disposition: uniquely here the tsaddiq names a trait of conduct alongside graciousness and mercy. Source (103) is unrecorded. Seat (104) resolves to none. Bearer (105) is the man - the God-fearer (inferred). Operation (106) is the core event: be righteous - in his dealings. Target (107) is 'in dealings' (inferred) - the righteousness shows in how he treats others. Manner (108) is none. Intensity (109), specifier (110), effect (111) and prohibition (113) are all absent. Coupling (112) as recorded reads 'internal:ib-state'; locus (116) pairs it with being gracious and merciful (v4). Discovery (114) sets it at v4: 'gracious, merciful, and righteous' - the uprightness of the God-fearer's conduct. Role (115) is characteristic. The full process: with no named source, the God-fearer is righteous in the way he deals with others - his righteousness set in a triad with grace and mercy, integrity read not as cold correctness but as one facet of a warm, generous character; the same man for whom light dawns in the dark is himself gracious, merciful, and right in his dealings.
narratives.story: The God-fearing man of this psalm is described with three words that belong together: gracious, merciful, and righteous. His righteousness is not a cold, rule-bound correctness - it stands right next to graciousness and mercy, part of one warm character. He is fair and upright in how he treats people, and that fairness comes wrapped in kindness. The passage will go on to show him giving generously to the poor; here it names the inner shape of the man behind that giving. Integrity, on this reading, is not severe. It is one face of a good-hearted person who is also gracious and merciful - right in his dealings because he is kind at his core.
narratives.variation_note: One of seventeen readings of 'righteous' (tsaddiq), sharing Psa 112:4 with the yashar reading. Distinctive here: the tsaddiq is a disposition of conduct set in a triad with grace and mercy - integrity as warm character, not the status-of-a-community that most tsaddiq readings carry. It reads righteousness as one facet of a gracious, merciful person's dealings.

narratives.narrative: The sense (101) is 'justice (mishpat)' - 'who conducts his affairs with justice'. Type (102) is disposition. Source (103) is unrecorded. Seat (104) resolves to none. Bearer (105) is the man - the God-fearer (inferred). Operation (106) is the core event: conduct affairs - with justice. Target (107) is 'with justice' (inferred) - fairness in his business. Manner (108) is none. Intensity (109), specifier (110), effect (111) and prohibition (113) are all absent. Coupling (112) as recorded reads 'internal:ib-state'; locus (116) pairs justice with dealing generously (v5). Discovery (114) sets it at v5: 'who conducts his affairs with justice' - the just ordering of the God-fearer's business, fairness in all dealings. Role (115) is characteristic. The full process: with no named source, the God-fearer runs his everyday business justly - integrity read at the level of ordinary commerce, justice as the fairness that governs a generous man's lending and dealing; not a courtroom virtue here but the honesty of a private life well-ordered, paired with his open-handed giving.
narratives.story: Justice, in this verse, comes down to earth - into a man's everyday business. It is well with the man who deals generously and lends, the psalm says, and who conducts his affairs with justice. This is not justice from a throne or a judge's bench; it is the plain fairness of someone running his own affairs honestly, lending without cheating, dealing squarely with everyone. And it sits right beside his generosity - he gives freely and he deals fairly, two sides of the same decent life. The passage brings integrity into ordinary transactions: the honest person is just not only in grand matters but in how he handles his money and his neighbours, day by day.
narratives.variation_note: Third of three readings of 'justice' (mishpat). Here at Psa 112:5 justice governs a man's private business dealings - fairness in ordinary commerce, paired with generous lending. It differs from Psa 72:1 (justice as a governing gift to the king) and Psa 106:3 (justice as the constant practice of the blessed). Here alone justice is scaled down to everyday private affairs, integrity in how a man handles his own transactions.

narratives.narrative: The sense (101) is 'righteous (tsaddiq)' - 'the righteous will never be moved'. Type (102) is status. Source (103) is unrecorded. Seat (104) resolves to none. Bearer (105) is the righteous (inferred). Operation (106) is the core event: never be moved - the immovable stability of the righteous. Target (107) is 'being steadfast' (inferred). Manner (108) is none. Intensity (109), specifier (110), effect (111) and prohibition (113) are all absent. Coupling (112) as recorded reads 'internal:ib-state'; locus (116) pairs it with being remembered forever (v6). Discovery (114) sets it at v6: 'For the righteous will never be moved' - the immovable stability of the righteous, rooted in God. Role (115) is characteristic. The full process: with no named source, the righteous will never be moved and will be remembered forever - integrity read as permanence in two directions, unshakeable in the present and unforgotten in the future; the settled steadiness of the God-fearer, whose firm heart (v7) trusts the LORD and so cannot be toppled.
narratives.story: Of the God-fearing man the psalm says two things about permanence: he will never be moved, and he will be remembered forever. He cannot be knocked off his footing in the present, and he will not be forgotten in the future. His heart is firm, trusting in the Lord, so bad news does not shake him and enemies do not topple him. Integrity here is stability that runs both ways - steady now, remembered later. The passage roots this immovability in his trust: because his confidence rests on God rather than on anything that can be taken from him, nothing can dislodge him. The honest, God-trusting life stands firm and leaves a name that lasts.
narratives.variation_note: One of seventeen readings of 'righteous' (tsaddiq). Here at Psa 112:6 the righteous 'will never be moved' - stability paired with lasting remembrance. It shares the 'never moved' promise with Psa 55:22, but there the steadiness answers the terror of betrayal, while here it flows from the God-fearer's firm, trusting heart and is coupled with being remembered forever. The same immovability, differently grounded.

narratives.story: The psalm repeats its refrain - his righteousness endures forever - but this time it says exactly what that righteousness looks like: he has scattered his wealth freely, given to the poor. The enduring rightness of this man is not a private feeling; it is money handed out to those in need. Generosity is the shape his lasting righteousness takes. And because of it, his horn is exalted in honour - he is lifted up and dignified. The passage ties three things together: giving to the poor, a righteousness that never expires, and honour that follows. Integrity here proves its permanence precisely by letting go of wealth - the open hand is the mark of the rightness that stands forever.
narratives.variation_note: Fifth of five readings of 'righteousness' (H6666, tsedaqah), echoing the refrain of v3 within the same psalm. Where v3 (H6666:righteousnes#4) set enduring righteousness against transient wealth, v9 shows it enacted in giving that wealth away; the same permanence, now embodied in generosity and crowned with honour.

narratives.story: You can hear where the righteous live. Glad songs of salvation are in the tents of the righteous - their homes ring with music, celebrating how the Lord's right hand has rescued them. Integrity here is not silent or grim; it sounds like singing. The just have been delivered, and their gratitude fills their dwellings with joyful noise about what God has done. The passage lets you locate the honest by the sound coming from their tents - not complaint, but celebration of salvation. Rescued by God, the righteous turn their households into places of song. Their thankfulness becomes something you can actually hear.

It shares Psalm 118 with the next reading (v20, the righteous entering God's gate); together they move from the joyful homes of the righteous to their entrance into the LORD's presence.

narratives.story: There is a gate, and not everyone goes through it. This is the gate of the Lord; the righteous shall enter through it. The psalmist asks for the gates of righteousness to be opened so he can go in and give thanks - and the ones who pass through are the just. Integrity here is the pass that admits you: the righteous alone enter God's presence to worship. The passage makes uprightness the qualification for coming in - not to earn a reward, but to be the kind of person who belongs on the other side of that gate. The honest are those who walk through into the place of thanksgiving.
narratives.variation_note: One of seventeen readings of 'righteous' (tsaddiq), the second in Psalm 118. Here at v20 the righteous enter the LORD's gate - integrity as the qualification for entrance into God's presence. It pairs with v15 (the righteous whose tents ring with salvation-songs): the psalm moves from the joyful homes of the righteous to their admission through the gate. It also echoes the entrance-theme of Psa 24:4 (clean hands and pure heart), where purity qualifies the worshipper to ascend.

narratives.story: The longest psalm in the Bible opens with a beatitude, and its first word is about integrity: blessed are those whose way is blameless, who walk in the law of the Lord. To be blameless here is to have a whole, faultless way of life - and the way it is kept whole is by walking in God's law. The passage sets this down as the very first note of a vast meditation on God's word: the happy life is the blameless life, and the blameless life is the one lived along the grain of God's instruction. Integrity is not vague goodness but a way shaped by the law, and the psalm calls those who walk it blessed.
narratives.variation_note: Fourth of five readings of 'blameless' (tamim). Here at Psa 119:1 blamelessness is pronounced blessed - the opening beatitude of the great law-psalm, blamelessness defined as walking in the LORD's law. It differs from Psa 18:23 (self-guarding), Psa 101:2 (resolved on), Psa 101:6 (required of others), and Psa 119:80 (pleaded for). Here alone it is declared blessed, and tied explicitly to keeping God's word.

(Note this is yashar under the H3476 key, distinct from the H3477 'upright' spanning the other psalms.)
narratives.story: The psalmist links two things: learning God's righteous rules, and praising him with an upright heart. I will praise you with an upright heart, he says, when I learn your righteous rules. Straightness of heart is the condition of real worship here - you cannot truly praise God with a crooked or divided heart. And that uprightness grows as he learns God's ways; the more he takes in God's righteous rules, the straighter his heart becomes, and the more genuine his praise. The passage ties integrity to worship at the root: honest praise comes from an honest heart, and an honest heart is shaped by learning what God calls right. Uprightness within makes the thanksgiving true.

narratives.narrative: The sense (101) is 'blameless (tamim)' - 'may my heart be blameless in your statutes'. Type (102) is disposition. Source (103) is unrecorded. Seat (104) resolves to none for the term, though the verse names the heart. Bearer (105) is the psalmist (inferred). Operation (106) is the core event: be blameless in heart - here pleaded for, not claimed. Target (107) is none recorded. Manner (108) is none. Intensity (109), specifier (110), effect (111) and prohibition (113) are all absent. Coupling (112) is paired within its char-arc across the psalm (inferred). Discovery (114) sets it at v80: 'May my heart be blameless in your statutes, that I may not be put to shame!' - the plea for a blameless heart. Role (115) is characteristic; locus (116) is internal:ib-state. The full process: from no named source, the psalmist prays that his heart be made blameless in God's statutes so that he not be put to shame - integrity read here as a request, not a possession; blamelessness is something he asks God to work in him, a whole heart sought as the safeguard against shame, the desire of one who knows he cannot simply produce it himself.
narratives.story: Unlike the confident 'I was blameless' of other psalms, this is a prayer, and a humble one: may my heart be blameless in your statutes, that I may not be put to shame. The psalmist does not claim to have a faultless heart; he asks God to give him one. Blamelessness here is something he longs for and requests, a whole heart shaped by God's word, sought as protection against the shame that would come if he failed. The passage shows integrity from the side of need - the honest desire of a person who knows he cannot manufacture a clean heart on his own, and so asks God to make his heart whole in keeping with his commands.
narratives.variation_note: Fifth of five readings of 'blameless' (tamim). Here at Psa 119:80 blamelessness is pleaded for - a request that God make the heart whole, guarding against shame. It differs sharply from Psa 18:23 (blamelessness actively kept by the self) and Psa 119:1 (blamelessness pronounced blessed): here the psalmist does not claim it but asks for it. The variation marks a shift from possession to petition - integrity as something sought from God rather than achieved.

narratives.story: The psalm promises the righteous a protected portion. The scepter of wickedness - the rule of the oppressor - shall not come to rest permanently on the land allotted to the righteous. Their inheritance is under God's guard. Wickedness may press in for a time, but it will not be allowed to settle down and stay over the just. Integrity here is a possession God shields: the honest hold their ground because he keeps oppression from taking root there. The passage gives the righteous a reason to hold on under pressure - the tyranny bearing down on them is temporary by God's decree, and their allotted place is finally safe in his keeping.
narratives.variation_note: One of seventeen readings of 'righteous' (tsaddiq), the first of two in Psa 125:3. Here the righteous hold their God-guarded land, protected from lasting oppression. It differs pointedly from the second reading in the same verse (H6662:righteou#17), which turns to the danger that the righteous, under unrelieved oppression, might themselves reach toward wrong. The one verse holds both the promise of protection and the warning about its purpose - lest the just be pushed into sin.

narratives.narrative: The sense (101) is 'righteous (tsaddiq)' - 'lest the righteous stretch out their hands to do wrong'. Type (102) is status. Source (103) is unrecorded. Seat (104) resolves to none. Bearer (105) is the righteous (inferred). Operation (106) is the core event, and it is the family's darkest: be tempted under pressure - the righteous, under unrelieved oppression, on the verge of reaching toward sin. Target (107) is 'toward wrong' (inferred) - the temptation bends them toward wrongdoing. Manner (108) is none. Intensity (109), specifier (110), effect (111) and prohibition (113) are all absent. Coupling (112) as recorded reads 'internal:ib-state'; locus (116) pairs the righteous with stretching out to wrong (v3). Discovery (114) sets it at v3: 'lest the righteous stretch out their hands to do wrong' - the just who, under unrelieved oppression, might themselves be tempted to reach toward sin. Role (115) is characteristic. The full process: with no named source, the reading exposes a vulnerability inside integrity itself - if oppression is allowed to rest too long on the righteous, even they may stretch out their hands to wrong; the very reason God limits the tyranny is to keep the just from being pushed past their integrity. Read at full weight: the righteous are not immune to being broken toward sin under enough pressure.
narratives.story: Here the psalm says something unusually honest about even good people. God will not let the oppressor's rule rest forever on the righteous - and it gives the reason: lest the righteous stretch out their hands to do wrong. In other words, if the pressure went on unrelieved, even the honest might crack and reach for something crooked. Integrity is not treated as unbreakable. Push good people hard enough, long enough, and they too can be bent toward sin. So God limits the tyranny partly to protect the character of the just themselves - to keep them from being broken past the point where they can stay honest. The passage looks squarely at the fact that even the righteous have a breaking point.
narratives.variation_note: One of seventeen readings of 'righteous' (tsaddiq), the second of two in Psa 125:3 - and the most striking in the whole family. Where nearly every other tsaddiq reading shows the righteous rewarded, vindicated, or steadfast, this one exposes their vulnerability: under unrelieved oppression even the righteous might reach toward wrong. It is the family's clearest descent-note, read at full weight. It pairs with #16 in the same verse (the righteous whose land God guards): God shields their portion precisely so their integrity is not broken.

narratives.narrative: The sense (101) is 'upright (yashar)' - 'those who are upright in their hearts'. Type (102) is disposition. Source (103) is unrecorded. Seat (104) resolves to none for the term, though the verse names the heart. Bearer (105) is the upright (inferred). Operation (106) is the core event: be upright - in heart. Target (107) is 'in heart' (inferred) - the uprightness is inward. Manner (108) is none. Intensity (109), specifier (110), effect (111) and prohibition (113) are all absent. Coupling (112) as recorded reads 'internal:ib-state'; locus (116) pairs the upright with the heart (v4). The full process: with no named source, the upright in heart are those to whom the psalmist prays God will do good - integrity read as inner rectitude that draws God's favour; set against those who 'turn aside to their crooked ways' (v5), the straight-hearted are marked off by the honesty of their inner life and prayed a blessing, the crooked handed over to judgment.
narratives.story: The psalm makes a simple prayer and draws a sharp line. Do good, O Lord, to those who are good, and to those who are upright in their hearts. On one side stand the straight-hearted, marked by an honest inner life; on the other, those who turn aside to crooked ways, whom the Lord leads off with the evildoers. Integrity here is a matter of the heart's direction - straight or bent - and the upright in heart are the ones the psalmist asks God to bless. The passage sorts people by inner rectitude and prays good for the honest. To be upright in heart is to be on the side that draws God's favour rather than his judgment.
narratives.variation_note: Tenth of ten readings of 'upright' (yashar). Here at Psa 125:4 the upright in heart are those prayed a blessing, set against the crooked who are led away in judgment. It closes the yashar series by returning to the inner seat - uprightness 'in their hearts' - and by sorting the upright from the crooked. Where the series began with the upright beholding God's face (11:7), it ends with them prayed God's good, integrity as the heart-direction that divides the blessed from the judged.

Seat (104) resolves to none. Bearer (105) is the priests (inferred). Operation (106) is the core event: be clothed with righteousness - in their service. The full process: with no named source, the priests are prayed to be clothed with righteousness - integrity read as vesture, a rightness worn like the garments of office that fits them for God's service; paired with the saints' shout of joy, the righteousness put on the ministers is the qualification for standing in God's presence to serve, character imagined as clothing.
narratives.story: As the ark is brought to its resting place, the psalm prays for those who will serve there: let your priests be clothed with righteousness. Righteousness here is pictured as clothing - a rightness the priests put on like their robes of office, the thing that makes them fit to minister before God. It is not enough to wear the vestments; they must be dressed in the virtue itself. And alongside it comes the answering joy: let your saints shout for joy. The passage imagines integrity as vesture - character worn as a garment, qualifying the ministers to stand in God's presence. Right living is the true robe of anyone who would serve at the altar.
narratives.variation_note: Fourth of four readings of 'righteousness' (H6664, tsedeq). Here at Psa 132:9 righteousness is priestly vesture - a rightness the ministers put on to be fit for service. It differs from Psa 18:20 (the self's own vindication reckoned from deliverance) and Psa 45:4/45:7 (the king's political programme and the object of his love). Here alone righteousness is imagined as clothing worn for God's service - integrity as the garment of those who minister.
